bioinfo.title: Adaptive Framework for Integrating Regulatory Pathways and Cellular Signaling in Single Cell Biology
bioinfo.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has transformed the study of cellular heterogeneity, enabling detailed characterization of cell types, regulatory programs, and disease-associated transcriptional changes. However, the growing number of computational methods for core analysis tasks introduces variability and limits reproducibility across datasets. In this dissertation, I present a generalizable computational framework for single-cell analysis that integrates regulatory pathways and cellular signaling to improve biological interpretability. First, I develop consensus-based methods for key scRNA-seq tasks, including cell clustering and gene regulatory network inference, leveraging a wisdom-of-crowds strategy to enhance performance across datasets. Second, I introduce novel approaches for cell-type-resolved marker gene selection and signaling-informed transcription factor activity estimation, incorporating both downstream gene expression and upstream cell–cell communication signals to better capture regulatory mechanisms. Finally, I apply state of the art single cell genomics analysis methods to disease contexts in neurology and cancer, using single-cell and spatial transcriptomics to uncover cell-type-specific signaling and transcriptional changes associated with disease progression and therapeutic response. Together, this work bridges methodological development and biomedical application, providing a unified framework for integrating cellular signaling and gene regulation in single-cell genomics.

bioinfo.title: CellPatch: a flexible and efficient framework for single-cell foundation models empowered by heuristic gene patching
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Foundation models have advanced single-cell omics analysis but often remain too complex for practical use. We present CellPatch, a lightweight foundation model combining cross-attention with heuristic gene patching to reduce computational complexity during pretraining and fine-tuning while enabling inspection of gene-attention patterns. Across single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets spanning multiple organs and tissue states, CellPatch achieves state-of-the-art performance on diverse prediction tasks. Its modular design supports linear, adapter-based and task-specific architectures, enabling CellPatch to be adapted to diverse biological tasks.

bioinfo.title: scRep: A Latent-Space Self-Distilled Foundation Model for Single-Cell Representation Learning
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Single-cell foundation models have shown strong potential for learning transferable representations from large-scale transcriptomic data. However, many existing approaches rely on reconstructing masked gene expression values, creating a potential mismatch between observation-space reconstruction and the goal of learning stable biological representations. This challenge is particularly relevant to single-cell RNA sequencing, where sparsity, incomplete gene detection, and technical variation can obscure the underlying biological state. Here, we introduce scRep, a compact latent-space self-distillation framework for single-cell representation learning. Rather than reconstructing raw expression values, scRep aligns differently perturbed views of the same cell through a momentum-updated teacher–student architecture, with self-distillation objectives at both the cell and gene levels. This representation-centered formulation encourages the model to capture biological information that remains stable across incomplete and perturbed transcriptomic observations. Using frozen representations without task-specific fine-tuning, scRep pretrained on approximately 2.8 million cells achieves the strongest overall performance across the evaluated frozen-representation benchmarks, demonstrating strong sample efficiency. A larger-scale scRep model pretrained on 30.72 million cells further demonstrates that the framework remains effective when scaled to a substantially larger and more diverse corpus. Beyond cell identity, scRep prioritizes established marker genes, recovers transcription factor–associated gene programs with cell-type-specific activity, and preserves continuous developmental structure that supports graph-based pseudotime inference. We further show that pretraining performance is closely associated with biological diversity: reducing redundant cells while improving cell-type coverage can match or exceed the performance of larger, less balanced training corpora. Together, these results establish latent-space self-distillation as an effective alternative to expression reconstruction for single-cell foundation modeling and suggest that efficient scaling depends not only on the number of cells, but also on the learning objective and the biological diversity of the pretraining corpus.

bioinfo.title: Evaluation of a deep generative computational framework under constrained conditions for multi-regional placental single-cell transcriptomic inference
LongAllele: a joint inference framework for allele-specific analysis on long-read bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Allele-specific analysis from RNA-seq is a powerful approach to characterize cis -regulatory effects. However, existing methods remain limited in both haplotype inference and allelic testing. Their haplotype-inference workflows separate variant calling, haplotype phasing, and read-haplotype assignment into sequential steps, failing to fully exploit within-read single-nucleotide variant (SNV) linkage information and propagating errors into downstream allelic analysis. At the testing stage, they ignore non-phasable reads lacking heterozygous SNVs, biasing calls and inflating false positives, and remain incomplete across gene-, isoform-, and local-event-level variant effects. Here, we present LongAllele, a statistical framework that employs an expectation-maximization algorithm to jointly infer heterozygous variants, haplotype structure, and read-haplotype assignments from long-read bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing. LongAllele further introduces phasability-aware testing that explicitly accounts for non-phasable reads, avoiding inflated false-positive calls when haplotype information is incomplete. It also enables comprehensive allelic testing across gene-level allele-specific expression (ASE), isoform-level allele-specific transcript usage (ASTU), and local-event-level haplotype-associated exon and junction usage (HAEU and HAJU), providing a multi-scale view of cis -regulation across biological contexts. We applied LongAllele to long-read RNA-seq datasets spanning GTEx (multi-tissue bulk), peripheral blood mononuclear cells (single-cell), human hippocampus (single-nucleus), and human cortex from two Alzheimer’s disease (AD) case-control cohorts (bulk, Oxford Nanopore and PacBio). LongAllele consistently revealed greater context dependence in expression-level than isoform-level allelic regulation across tissues, cell types, and disease states, and pinpointed high-impact regulatory variants including rare splice-site mutations missed by standalone variant callers. It further showed that purifying selection constrains allelic imbalance at both gene and isoform levels and resolved AD-associated variant effects in individual transcriptomes across long-read platforms.

bioinfo.title: FastCCC: a permutation-free framework for scalable, robust, and reference-based cell-cell communication analysis in single cell transcriptomics studies
bioinfo.abstract: Detecting cell-cell communications (CCCs) in single-cell transcriptomics studies is fundamental for understanding the function of multicellular organisms. Here, we introduce FastCCC, a permutation-free framework that enables scalable, robust, and reference-based analysis for identifying critical CCCs and uncovering biological insights. FastCCC relies on fast Fourier transformation-based convolution to compute p-values analytically without permutations, introduces a modular algebraic operation framework to capture a broad spectrum of CCC patterns, and can leverage atlas-scale single cell references to enhance CCC analysis on user-collected datasets. To support routine reference-based CCC analysis, we constructed the first human CCC reference panel, encompassing 19 distinct tissue types, over 450 unique cell types, and approximately 16 million cells. We demonstrate the advantages of FastCCC across multiple datasets, most of which exceed the analytical capabilities of existing CCC methods. In real datasets, FastCCC reliably captures biologically meaningful CCCs, even in highly complex tissue environments, including differential interactions between endothelial and immune cells linked to COVID-19 severity, dynamic communications in thymic tissue during T-cell development, as well as distinct interactions in reference-based CCC analysis. As single-cell datasets scale to millions of cells, analyzing cell-cell communication becomes computationally challenging. Here, authors present FastCCC, a fast, permutation-free framework that enables scalable CCC analysis and provides a comprehensive human CCC reference panel.

bioinfo.title: SPECHTacle: An Efficient Detection and Visualization of Cell Specific Regulation in Single Cell-Based Experiments Using a Novel Combinatorial Computational Tool
bioinfo.abstract: ABSTRACT Herein, we describe SPECHTacle, a novel computational tool affording the ability to efficiently visualize and delineate the specific cellular population(s) impacted by an experimental paradigm utilizing heterogeneous cell-based samples. SPECHTacle can be employed to efficiently determine, in a cell specific manner, the populations preferentially impacted by treatments, drugs, injuries, disease states, and/or development within datasets continuously being generated across nearly countless subfields in molecular biology. SPECHTacle accomplishes this task by harnessing the power of Waddington optimal transport analysis and Shannon entropy in a combinatorial fashion to distinguish cell populations preferentially altered due to nearly any experimental paradigm and generates a visual representation of cellular entropy (i.e. change) across entire datasets. Ultimately, this allows for efficient determination of specific populations preferentially impacted by an experimental paradigm and identifies populations to target for downstream analyses employing quantitative measurements. We propose that SPECHTacle represents an immediately useful computational tool with the potential to be integrated into single cell-based workflows and greatly enhance the efficiency of both manual and machine-based learning workflows.

bioinfo.title: Reusability report: multi-sample omics network inference operates in distinct robustness regimes defined by prior knowledge and data availability
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Knowledge-constrained network inference enables the reconstruction of regulatory programmes from high-dimensional biological data, yet the conditions under which shared and context-specific structures can be reliably identified remain poorly understood. Pablo Rodriguez-Mier et al. recently introduced CORNETO, a framework for multi-sample constrained inference. Here we reproduce, evaluate and extend CORNETO in terms of robustness, identifiability and bias–variance trade-offs. Using dynamic haematopoiesis and stable cortical datasets, we systematically assess four network reconstruction paradigms while preserving the original method-specific evaluation procedures and benchmark definitions. We show that multi-sample inference generally improves robustness and reproducibility, although gains in predictive performance depend on biological context and the completeness of the prior network. To enhance stability, we introduce bootstrap aggregation and selective re-expansion strategies that improve consensus robustness and recovery while preserving context-specific signals without modifying the underlying optimization scheme or sacrificing generality. Across datasets and methods, our results reveal distinct inference regimes governed by sample availability, prior knowledge and regularization. Together, these findings position network reconstruction as a regime-dependent learning problem and provide practical principles for robust multi-sample biological network inference.

bioinfo.title: A multi-layer framework for computational cancer epigenomics
bioinfo.abstract: Cancer epigenomics has become central to understanding tumor initiation, progression, heterogeneity, and therapeutic response. High-throughput profiling technologies including bisulfite sequencing, chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq), assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (ATAC-seq), and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) generate complex, multi-dimensional datasets that require robust computational frameworks for meaningful interpretation. This review outlines key bioinformatics workflows in cancer epigenomics, including data preprocessing, quality control, sequence alignment, signal detection, and differential analysis. While epigenomic data provide a mechanistic regulatory foundation, their full interpretive value emerges through integration with genomic, transcriptomic, and clinical data within computational oncology frameworks. Accordingly, we emphasize integrative modeling approaches that combine multi-omics data to uncover regulatory mechanisms, identify biomarkers, and define disease-associated molecular subtypes. Machine learning methods are increasingly applied for classification, prognosis prediction, and therapeutic response modeling; however, challenges remain in model interpretability, reproducibility, and external validation. We further highlight critical analytical limitations, including data heterogeneity, tumor complexity, lack of standardized workflows, and the persistent gap between association and biological mechanism. Emerging advances in single-cell epigenomics, spatial profiling, and explainable AI offer new opportunities to refine biological insight and clinical translation. Importantly, we propose a structured multi-layer interpretation framework that links computational outputs across data-level processing, epigenomics-informed integrative regulatory modeling, and multi-omics-informed clinical interpretation. This framework differs from existing pipelines by explicitly constraining how information is transformed across analytical layers, enabling traceable and mechanistically interpretable clinical inference.

bioinfo.title: Clifti-GPT: privacy-preserving federated fine-tuning and transferable inference of foundation models on clinical single-cell data.
bioinfo.abstract: Foundation models have demonstrated immense value for scRNA-seq analysis, but their fine-tuning or inference on heterogeneous, privacy-sensitive clinical cohorts is governed by strict data protection policies, which often prohibit centralization. We introduce Clifti-GPT, a privacy-preserving federated framework based on secure multi-party computation (SMPC) that enables collaborative model training and transferable inference, where zero-shot predictions are performed across decentralized clinical repositories by securely aggregating local statistics rather than transferring data embeddings, without sharing patient data, clinical-level statistics, or models. Built upon the scGPT foundation model, Clifti-GPT achieves performance within 4% of centralized scGPT baselines in accuracy, precision, recall, and macro-F1 for cell type classification and reference mapping across six datasets. Furthermore, it demonstrates rapid convergence in terms of communication rounds, reaching 99% of centralized performance on cell type classification in at most two federated rounds on two evaluated datasets, and scales robustly to 30 clients with less than 2% accuracy loss on a large-scale federated cell type classification setting. Our analysis shows that batch effects impact both Clifti-GPT and centralized baseline, while correction leads to similar results across evaluation metrics in heterogeneous settings for both models. Together, these results indicate that Clifti-GPT enables effective fine-tuning and application of single-cell foundation models across distributed clinical datasets in a manner that is GDPR-compatible by design and addresses real-world privacy and institutional data-governance requirements.

bioinfo.title: ComicGTN infers disease-associated rare cell states from single-cell multiomic data using DNA sequence–augmented graph transformer networks
bioinfo.abstract: Single-cell multiomic technology makes it possible to profile both the transcriptome and epigenome within individual cells. The detection of rare cell states from such data is crucial for exploring novel disease biomarkers with clinical potential. However, existing methods typically focus on the gene and peak counts while ignoring the underlying genomic sequence at accessible sites. Here, we propose ComicGTN, an innovative computational framework that integrates single-cell multiomic data with DNA sequence information via enhanced graph transformer networks to accurately identify rare cell clusters. ComicGTN consistently outperforms nine state-of-the-art methods in identifying rare cells across multiple complex scenarios. In mouse breast cancer data, ComicGTN detects several functionally distinct immune subpopulations. In cerebral cortex of epilepsy patients, it uncovers oligodendrocytes undergoing particular differentiation states. For polycystic kidney disease patient–derived organoids, ComicGTN elaborates pathological pathways in a captured rare glomerular subgroup. Overall, ComicGTN accelerates the localization of disease-associated rare cell populations, facilitating the derivation of clinical insights in development and disease progression.

bioinfo.title: PertDiffBench: Benchmarking Diffusion Models for Single-Cell Perturbation Response Prediction
bioinfo.abstract: Abstract Diffusion models are increasingly used to predict transcriptional responses to perturbations, but whether they improve on simpler generative and representation-based baselines remains unclear. Existing evaluations often do not separate the effects of model architecture, input representation, biological context and metric choice, making it difficult to determine where diffusion-based methods are useful. Here we introduce PertDiffBench, a standardized benchmark for diffusion-based transcriptomic perturbation prediction across single-cell and bulk RNA-seq datasets. PertDiffBench evaluates diffusion-based models across three complementary evaluation settings: standard prediction in known single-cell contexts and bulk perturbation conditions, generalization to unseen cell types, species, drugs and intermediate time points, and stress tests of feature dimensionality, input representation, noise type and gene ordering. Across these settings, diffusion models did not show a consistent advantage. scGen remained a strong baseline in common prediction tasks, whereas scDiffusion was the most competitive diffusion-based method in several generalization settings. Temporal imputation showed a different pattern, with a simple DDPM operating directly in expression space outperforming more specialized models. Stress tests showed that performance was model dependent and sensitive to feature dimensionality, encoder choice, noise type and gene ordering. Pretrained encoders did not consistently improve performance, with the classical scVI representation slightly exceeding STATE in seen-condition and unseen-cell-type settings. These results indicate that diffusion-model performance in perturbation response prediction depends strongly on task design and representation choice. PertDiffBench provides a practical framework for evaluating these models under biologically varied and stress-tested conditions.

ml.title: Multimodal Masked Diffusion Autoencoder for Modeling Impaired Driving
ml.abstract: Human cognitive state (e.g., distraction, stress), gaze, and behavior interact with the driving environment in subtle ways that AI could use to assist drivers, but ground-truth labels for human cognitive state levels are costly to obtain at scale. We propose a multimodal masked-diffusion autoencoder, ID-MAE, that adds a self-supervised objective to impairment prediction: alongside predicting the impairment label as a masked token, it reconstructs masked gaze and trajectory. To probe the effects of different modalities and types of impairments on model inference, we introduce DIVERT, a driving-simulator dataset containing 103 hours of driving data (n = 109) with ten impairment inductions spanning cognitive, visual, and emotional states, recorded with gaze, vehicle state, and scene video. We demonstrate how ID-MAE affords significant improvements in impairment inference results on both the DIVERT dataset and existing datasets, and enables strong results in additional tasks, such as trajectory and gaze prediction. For location-matched pairs, our model achieves a paired AUC of 0.706 for impairment detection on DIVERT, compared to 0.590 without reconstruction loss, improving over existing baselines. We probe the design space in terms of input modalities, masking scheme, positional encoding, attention mechanism, and decoding. We also investigate the interaction between various impairments in training and inference, demonstrating that visually demanding distractions are separable from cognitive distractions. Code and data will be available upon acceptance.

ml.title: ScanFlow: Context-Aware Fixation Transition Flow Matching for Generative Scanpath Prediction
ml.abstract: Scanpath prediction aims to generate realistic fixation sequences conditioned on visual scenes and tasks, capturing human visual attention. Recent studies model inherent gaze variability using generative techniques, particularly diffusion models. While effective, existing methods treat scanpath generation as modeling of holistic sequence distributions, in which contextual information is used as a conditioning signal rather than explicitly embedded in fixation sequences. This formulation overlooks that scanpaths are inherently composed of spatial-temporal, context-dependent fixation transitions, which may limit fine-grained coherence. To address this limitation, we propose a fixation-level generative paradigm for scanpath prediction. Unlike existing methods that capture coarse global structures, we model scanpaths as sequential fixation transitions, enabling fine-grained dependency and dynamic modeling across fixations, thereby naturally balancing coherence and variability. Specifically, we introduce a new framework, ScanFlow, with three key components. First, we integrate spatial-temporal and contextual semantics to construct scanpath representations that capture transition dependencies to preserve coherence. Second, we use flow matching with semantics-aligned contrastive regularization to model stochastic transition dynamics, thereby capturing structured and context-aware variability. Third, we adopt a flexible autoregressive strategy that balances deterministic and stochastic components to sequentially generate diverse yet context-coherent fixation sequences. Extensive experiments across five datasets with various viewing scenarios demonstrate the effectiveness of ScanFlow for high-quality and realistic scanpath generation.

ml.title: Generative structure-guided denoising diffusion probabilistic model for MR to CT image synthesis in radiotherapy planning
ml.abstract: Abstract Objective . Radiotherapy (RT) planning uses magnetic resonance (MR) imaging for soft tissue information, while computerized tomography (CT) imaging is necessary for dose calculation. Synthetic CTs generated from MR images (MRI) streamline the clinical workflow by reducing the need for an actual CT acquisition while minimizing radiation exposure, enabling adaptive RT workflows. The objective of this study is to propose a new RT planning model combining stable structure-guided denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) with MRI conditioning, for generating synthetic CT (sCT) images. Approach . The model combines a hybrid network architecture with a dynamic guidance mechanism, conditioned on MR images, to direct the reverse diffusion process and preserve structural details. The model integrates both a denoising and a refinement network: the denoising network predicts and progressively removes the noise added during the forward diffusion process, while the guidance strength adapts at each timestep based on the noise level. This adaptive guidance mechanism uses a non-linear formulation that satisfies noise constraints, optimizing the denoising process while preserving structural integrity. The training process includes a weighted structure-guided loss function that combines the DDPM noise loss with a dynamic guidance regularizer term for sCT image generation via noise prediction, along with a reconstruction loss for refinement. Main results . Evaluated on three paired MR/CT datasets (head and neck (HaN), as well as brain), our model outperforms recent MR to CT synthesis models, showing the best performance in image quality based on the mean absolute error in Hounsfield units, as well as improved peak signal-to-noise ratio, structural similarity index and gradient magnitude similarity deviation compared to other DDPM and generative adversarial network approaches. When comparing tumor segmentation quality, it achieves the best results in Dice score (0.76 ± 0.04), Hausdorff distance (7.9 ± 2.0), intersection over union (0.69 ± 0.04), geometric consistency index (0.84 ± 0.04) and precision-recall index (PRI) (0.88 ± 0.03) for segmented tumor regions in the generated sCT images. Finally, it achieves the best mean square error of 10.1 ± 2.6 Gray (Gy) in the head-and-neck cohort, when evaluating dose planning on sCT, with a conformity index of 0.61 ± 0.02 and a homogeneity index of 0.10 ± 0.02. Significance . Performance shows promise in integration for RT in HaN, as well as in brain cancers.

ml.title: Deposition-Based 3D Generative Modeling: A Framework for Three-Dimensional Object Generation Through Gas-Phase Particle Deposition, Local Adsorption, and Branching Growth
ml.abstract: Three-dimensional generative modeling has advanced through approaches such as 3D diffusion models, neural radiance fields (NeRF), 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), point-cloud generation, and voxel-based generation. Despite their differences in representation and optimization, these approaches generally construct objects by predicting, refining, or reconstructing spatial representations. This paper proposes Deposition-Based 3D Generative Modeling (D3GM), a conceptual framework that formulates three-dimensional object generation as a dynamic process of gas-phase particle transport, local surface adsorption, solid deposition, and branching growth. Inspired by physical deposition and frost formation, D3GM represents a target object as the outcome of successive deposition events rather than solely as a directly predicted geometric structure. A three-dimensional environment contains mobile candidate particles, spatially varying deposition conditions, local attraction fields, and evolving solid structures. Particles move through the environment, interact with existing surfaces, and become incorporated into the developing object according to learned or prescribed deposition rules. Local growth conditions determine whether deposition thickens existing structures, initiates new branches, reinforces selected regions, or terminates growth. A learned controller can adapt particle transport, adsorption probability, branching behavior, and deposition intensity to satisfy target geometry and appearance constraints. The resulting structure can be represented as a point cloud, voxel field, mesh, implicit surface, or a collection of three-dimensional Gaussian primitives. This paper defines the conceptual architecture, mathematical formulation, generation algorithm, training strategy, evaluation protocol, and principal research challenges of D3GM. The framework is proposed as a research direction, not as an experimentally validated method. Its potential contribution is the explicit use of deposition events and local growth dynamics as the primary generative mechanism for three-dimensional structures.

ml.title: Censored Flow Matching for Synthetic Time-to-Event Generation
ml.abstract: Generating time-to-event data is increasingly important in survival analysis, but it remains statistically challenging because event times are often censored and thus prevent flexible generative modeling. To fill this gap, we propose a novel method called censored flow matching (CFM), aiming at providing a flexible flow-based generative mechanism for synthesizing time-to-event data as well as learning their corresponding probabilistic densities. Unlike existing methods, CFM does not rely on survival likelihoods to handle censoring, but instead exploits the monotonicity property of differential flows to address censoring via pullback sampling. Under this framework, we implement an alternating procedure between pullback sampling and CFM steps, leading to a flow-based expectation--maximization (EM) algorithm tailored for time-to-event inference. Under mild distributional conditions, we establish the convergence of CFM to the true event-time distribution as the EM iterations proceed. We then apply CFM to generate time-to-event data and estimate their probabilistic densities, where the observed censoring time can be incorporated to provide truncated sampling or truncated density estimation for survival inference. Through extensive simulation studies, we demonstrate the benefits of CFM for complex and large-scale data generation. Finally, we apply CFM to analyze data from the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN) and the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV), showcasing its benefits for synthetic and predictive survival analyses in terms of data fidelity, predictive performance, and empirical privacy characteristics.

ml.title: Bridging Generative and Discriminative Noisy-Label Learning via Direction-Agnostic EM Formulation
ml.abstract: Although noisy-label learning is often approached with discriminative methods for simplicity and speed, generative modeling offers a principled alternative by capturing the joint mechanism that produces features, clean labels, and corrupted observations. However, prior work typically (i) introduces extra latent variables and heavy image generators that bias training toward reconstruction, (ii) fixes a single data-generating direction (Y →X or X →Y), limiting adaptability, and (iii) assumes a uniform prior over clean labels, ignoring instance-level uncertainty. Here, we propose a single-stage, EM-style framework for generative noisy-label learning that is direction-agnostic and avoids explicit image synthesis. First, we derive a single Expectation Maximization (EM) objective whose E-step specializes to either causal orientation without changing the overall optimization objective. Second, we replace the intractable p(X | Y) with a dataset-normalized discriminative proxy computed using a discriminative classifier on the finite training set, retaining the structural benefits of generative modeling at much lower cost. Third, we introduce Partial-Label Supervision (PLS), an instance specific prior over clean labels that balances coverage and uncertainty, improving data-dependent regularization. Across standard vision and natural language processing (NLP) noisy label benchmarks, our method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, lower transition-matrix estimation error, and substantially less training computation than current generative and discriminative baselines. Code: https://github.com/lfb-1/GNL.

ml.title: Task Convergent Flow Matching for Generative Robotics
ml.abstract: Successful manipulation requires the manipulated objects to progress toward a desired task outcome. Generative policies can produce plausible robot motions without ensuring this progress, allowing successive action chunks to stall or undo earlier changes to the scene. We introduce a task-centric inference-time refinement framework for flow matching policies that evaluates candidate action chunks through parallel physics-based rollouts and searches for motions satisfying sufficient conditions for task convergence. Task-level performance funnels bound temporary regressions while requiring net progress over each chunk. We establish sufficient conditions under which repeated funnel satisfaction yields convergence throughout execution, and use interval-wise Lipschitz bounds to verify continuous-time funnel satisfaction from sampled rollouts. To accommodate contact-rich hybrid dynamics, we refine the flow's source seeds using derivative-free Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES), constrained to radial quantile bands of the source distribution to help retain the learned motion prior. This formulation supports both Euclidean and pose-valued Riemannian Flow Matching (RMFM) policies. On PushT and three-cube stacking, refinement raises success from 31.3% to 88.5% and from 77.0% to 86.0%. On PushT, whose coverage score responds continuously to the motion of the block, a learned funnel lowers the average maximum loss of achieved progress by 19% relative to constraining the endpoint of each chunk alone, at a similar success rate. With the radial band, 11.3% of the executed motion windows are out of distribution, a rate within the range of held-out demonstrations, compared with 34.1% for an unconstrained search.

ml.title: Distribution-Based Regularization for Reward Fine-Tuning Diffusion and Flow Models
ml.abstract: Reward fine-tuning is an effective way to adapt pretrained diffusion and flow-matching models to downstream objectives, but aggressive optimization often leads to mode collapse and distributional drift. Existing methods attempt to control this drift with reverse-KL regularization, implemented as an $\ell_2$ penalty on the velocity field; however, this functions by indirectly constraining sampling dynamics rather than directly acting on the generated distribution. To address this, we propose DFR (Distributional Functional Rewards), which augments the task reward with a distribution-dependent, per-sample reward that acts explicitly on the generated distribution. Formally, we generalize the KL-regularized objective from expected rewards, which are linear in the model's distribution, to convex functionals of it. The first variation of this objective defines an effective, distribution-dependent reward that directly penalizes deviation from the pretrained distribution. This formulation yields additive per-sample rewards for the Fréchet distance (FD), maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), and DreamSim diversity, recovering several recently proposed rewards as special cases. Across various text-to-image fine-tuning tasks, DFR matches the peak reward of KL-tuned baselines while increasing diversity by up to 29% at equal or lower drift.

ml.title: Inertial Video World Models
ml.abstract: The physical world has inertia: it evolves from what already exists rather than being recreated at every instant. However, many existing video world models lack an explicit mechanism for inertial state evolution, leaving the continuity of motion and structure implicit in video prediction. During autoregressive rollouts, repeated reconstruction can accumulate errors and destabilize the predicted dynamics. To address this limitation, we introduce InertialWorld, an Inertial Video World Model that makes inertia a structural prior for autoregressive prediction: existing scene evidence is carried across time rather than reconstructed at every step. Central to this formulation is Inertial Memory, which turns memory from passive predictive context into an evolving video state with two complementary views: a dense Eulerian grid preserves scene-aligned evidence, while persistent Lagrangian carriers bind local content to learned canonical coordinates. At each step, the model transports the carrier content according to action-conditioned motion, predicts the complete next video state from the transported carriers and dense grid, and uses a learned gate to combine transported and newly predicted content into the memory for the next step. Extensive experiments across multiple domains, including robot manipulation, 3D game simulation, and open-world navigation, demonstrate that InertialWorld achieves competitive autoregressive prediction performance against strong video world model baselines. Codes link: https://github.com/YuanGao-YG/InertialWorld

ml.title: Generalized Prediction Set with Bandit Feedback
ml.abstract: In high-stakes environments where uncertainties abound, set-valued prediction offers a cautious and robust mechanism by presenting multiple potential labels as the prediction for each test instance to mitigate the potential risk associated with prediction errors. Yet, integrating this paradigm with out-of-distribution (OOD) detection remains scarcely explored in such settings as online learning with bandit feedback. The bandit feedback mechanism informs the learner about the correctness of the pulled arm/action instead of the explicit ground truth label, leaving the true class label unknown when an incorrect action is taken. To address this challenge, we introduce BanditGPS which conducts set-valued prediction with OOD detection in the bandit feedback setting, using an estimation to the ground truth of class labels. BanditGPS achieves three objectives: render small/informative prediction sets, enhance the OOD detection performance, and control the recall for all normal classes to meet prescribed requirements. Our approach is characterized by the loss function, which trades off between high OOD detection and small prediction sets. Theoretically, we prove that the convergence rate of the regret is $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-1/2})$. The empirical results further show that BanditGPS effectively controls the recalls with promising performances on OOD detection and informative prediction.

ml.title: Bridging Efficiency and Scalability in Generative Modeling
ml.abstract: Generative modeling has progressed from adversarial frameworks to diffusion and flow-based processes that now achieve state-of-the-art results across many domains. As these models have grown more capable, they have also sharpened a practical tension: the methods that deliver the highest quality often demand substantial cost in training, sampling, or deployment. We argue that the tradeoff between efficiency (strong results at lower computational cost) and scalability (improved quality with additional computation) is not absolute. Across six contributions spanning adversarial, diffusion, and flow-based models, we show that, although these objectives are often treated as competing, better objective design, inference-time search, and distillation can in important settings make generative systems both more efficient and more scalable. The first part of the thesis develops efficient training formulations. In adversarial generative modeling, we show that standard discriminator objectives exhibit alignment instability: the generator receives nonzero gradients even when it has already matched the data distribution, causing unnecessary oscillation. We introduce pairwise discriminators that eliminate this failure mode by making the aligned state stationary regardless of discriminator quality. We further develop Adversarial Support Alignment, replacing full distribution matching with the weaker but sufficient objective of support matching for domain adaptation under label shift. Turning to diffusion models, we introduce the Stable Target Field, which replaces the single-sample score estimation target with an importance-weighted average over a reference batch, substantially reducing target variance at high noise levels and accelerating convergence. We also present PFGM++, a unified framework connecting diffusion and Poisson flow models through a tunable augmented dimension that controls the tradeoff between training ease and sampling robustness. The second part introduces Inference-Time Scaling for diffusion models. We show that generation quality can continue to improve even after the gains from additional denoising steps have largely saturated by formulating inference as a search problem: candidate noises and trajectories are evaluated with learned verifiers, and test-time compute yields further quality gains. This establishes a new scaling axis for diffusion models, parallel to recent work on test-time compute in large language models. The final part bridges efficiency and scalability through distillation. While inference-time search produces high-quality outputs, it is too costly for practical deployment. We present FreeFlow, a data-free method for distilling flow models that addresses what we term Teacher-Data Mismatch: the gap between the data-noised intermediates used in standard distillation and the distributions encountered along the teacher's actual generating trajectories. By anchoring distillation at the prior (the unique point where these two processes must agree) and training through a predictor-corrector framework, FreeFlow distills the teacher into a single-function-evaluation student and achieves state-of-the-art one-step results without external data. The resulting model can also serve as a fast proxy for inference-time search, showing how efficient distillation can make scalable inference more practical. Together, these contributions show that efficiency and scalability in generative modeling need not always oppose one another: better formulations can improve stability and robustness, inference-time search can convert additional compute into better outputs, and efficient distillation can make those gains practical.

ml.title: LoopPrune: Recurrent Pruning for Looped Diffusion Transformers
ml.abstract: Looped diffusion Transformers reuse shared blocks to deepen computation and match larger models with fewer parameters, reducing storage and deployment burdens. Yet repeated attention and MLP computations remain costly. Pruning reduces storage and computation by removing redundant parameters or units. Training-free methods struggle to resolve recurrent contributions, while training-based methods lack explicit constraints on position-specific errors affecting later inputs and final outputs. We propose LoopPrune, a pruning and recovery framework addressing these requirements. Recurrent importance estimation combines shared-removal effects and position variation to select a shared structure; shared reconstruction pools recurrent input statistics to compensate weights. Loop-position recovery compares complete denoising predictions at identical student states and matches text guidance, updating all student parameters against a fixed dense teacher. Extensive experiments across four open-source models, six benchmarks, and three pruning paradigms demonstrate effectiveness. At 30% structured parameter pruning, Looped-DiT B/16 retains 93.14% of dense six-benchmark average accuracy, exceeding the best baseline by 9.49%. Across PyTorch, vLLM-Omni, and SGLang Diffusion, pruned SDXSv3 reduces peak allocated GPU memory by 34.36-44.64% and accelerates denoising 1.46-1.74x over dense models.

ml.title: Mean-field Token Steering
ml.abstract: We consider stochastic token steering through a deep stack of transformer layers as a mean-field control problem for an interacting particle system on the unit sphere, where interactions arise from the attention mechanism. In the mean-field limit, the token population evolves via a controlled integro-partial differential equation where the feedback control acts as a corrective vector field guiding the population toward an aggregate configuration of tokens in the representation space. We deduce the minimum effort control to accomplish this task over a fixed time horizon interpreted as normalized layer depth. We show that the resulting controlled dynamics for the token population can be understood as a mean-field Schrödinger bridge adapted to the sphere geometry. Building on this, we propose a novel generalization of the dynamic Sinkhorn recursion to compute the consistent token evolution. Numerical experiments confirm that the proposed approach achieves exact steering of the token population.

ml.title: Doob-Based Generative Policy Optimization
ml.abstract: Diffusion and flow models provide expressive policy classes for robotic and sequential decision-making systems. However, their action likelihoods are generally intractable, limiting the direct use of widely adopted policy optimization methods such as PPO and GRPO. We propose Doob Policy Optimization (DoobPO), a framework that leverages Doob's $h$-transform for likelihood-free reinforcement learning fine-tuning of generative policies. DoobPO separates policy improvement from generative policy learning. It first learns a lightweight ratio model that represents the desired policy update, and then distills the resulting ratio-tilted target policy into the generative policy via conditional drift matching. This formulation applies uniformly to both diffusion and flow policies and supports a broad family of policy improvement rules, including PPO and GRPO. We prove that the practical conditional drift matching objective is gradient-equivalent to the ideal Doob drift matching objective. We further show that the induced diffusion process solves an endpoint-constrained stochastic optimal control problem. This establishes that it achieves the minimum-energy modification required to realize the desired policy tilt. Across MuJoCo continuous-control benchmarks, DoobPO achieves strong performance against competitive diffusion- and flow-policy baselines, showing a principled and practical route to RL fine-tuning for generative policies.

ml.title: Dynamics-Aligned Representation Learning under Induced Partial Observability
ml.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) has enabled sample-efficient learning of continuous control policies from high-dimensional observations through learned latent dynamics models. These models are typically trained with observation reconstruction objectives, which provide strong supervision but can bias representations toward visual fidelity leading to an undertrained prior and unreliable long-horizon predictions. We propose a stochastic gating mechanism that induces controlled partial observability during training by sampling a spatial binary mask from a Beta--Bernoulli random field and applying it to the raw observation. The gate probability is resampled at each time step, exposing the encoder to conditions ranging from near-total occlusion to near-full visibility. Integration of our method requires minimal architectural changes from existing dynamics models: the gated observation and the binary mask are channel-wise concatenated and passed to the encoder as a single augmented input, with no modifications to the broader training pipeline. We evaluate the proposed approach on a set of pixel-based continuous control tasks selected from the DeepMind Control Suite. Using model predictive control for evaluation, which relies solely on open-loop model rollouts, we show that stochastic gating improves planning performance and data efficiency across tasks. Further analysis demonstrates that performance is robust to the spatial scale of the mask, and a balanced observability during training outperforms configurations biased toward either sparser or denser observations.

SAM operates far from home: eigenvalue regularization as a dynamical phenomenon
As Student Rollouts Continue, Visual Backdoors Keep Growing
ml.abstract: Conventional knowledge distillation can facilitate the propagation of backdoors from teacher models to student models. However, how this risk manifests in On-Policy Distillation (OPD) remains insufficiently studied. OPD has recently emerged as an important post-training paradigm for Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Unlike traditional offline distillation, OPD does not require teacher-generated responses. Instead, it uses the teacher's probability distributions to supervise response trajectories generated online by the student. Since the initial student model typically generates benign responses and receives no explicit supervision from malicious target responses, OPD appears to offer some inherent resistance to backdoor propagation. In this paper, we challenge this intuition and reveal a more subtle risk of visual backdoor propagation in OPD. Through experiments across multiple model families and datasets, together with theoretical analysis, we identify three main findings. First, unlike the relatively gradual propagation observed in traditional offline distillation, backdoors rarely emerge in OPD at low poisoning ratios. However, the attack success rate rapidly approaches 100% once a critical threshold is exceeded. Second, backdoor propagation does not depend on explicit malicious responses. Instead, it is driven by the continuous accumulation of anomalous probability mass assigned by the teacher. Finally, based on these findings, we propose a novel trigger design that enables visual backdoor propagation with zero explicit trigger injection. These findings further reveal an overlooked mechanism of backdoor propagation in OPD and highlight its potential security risks.

ml.title: BRepA: Graph-Based B-Rep Pretraining for Unified CAD Understanding and Generation
ml.abstract: Boundary representation (B-Rep) of CAD models encodes geometric primitives and their relations as a graph structure, enabling efficient shape modeling within CAD software. Learning on B-Reps for downstream tasks, such as segmentation and novel shape generation, requires specialized neural network designs. Moreover, performance improvements and accelerated training can be achieved with effective pretraining strategies, which is particularly important for tasks with limited labeled B-Rep data. In this paper, we introduce BRepA, a unified self-supervised pretraining framework that explicitly reconstructs both the geometry and topology of B-Rep objects via graph-based modeling. By learning from large-scale unlabeled CAD data only once, BRepA produces representations that generalize across tasks and significantly enhance both discriminative and generative learning. On segmentation tasks, BRepA demonstrates remarkable data efficiency. For instance, with only 1% labeled samples, BRepA pretraining improves mIoU by 32.52% compared to models trained from scratch. On generative tasks, aligning diffusion model representations with pretrained BRepA features substantially accelerates convergence, achieving nearly 2 times faster training while improving generation quality under the same computational budget, despite the diffusion model being roughly 20 times larger than BRepA. Overall, our results show that geometry- and topology-aware B-Rep pretraining provides a powerful foundation for both understanding and generating CAD structures, serving as a versatile representation backbone for diverse downstream applications. We will release the code to facilitate future research.

ml.title: Homogeneous pursuit in $β$ model
ml.abstract: Data in forms of networks has been encountered in various prevalent fields at the arrival of big data era. To unveil and recover the true model with core units with numerous links, the $β$-model under sparsity constraint is proposed to meet the expectation of statisticians and engineers. Not only does this network model inherit spectacular property from the Erdős-Rényi model, but also exhibits degree heterogeneity through tuning sparsity parameter $s$. In this paper, we propose Homogeneous Pursuit (HP), an $\ell_0$-constrained maximum likelihood estimation method implemented through a primal-dual algorithm. To ease the harshness of computation, we find the surrogate function of the corresponding objective function to derive Majorization Minimization algorithm through the primal-dual process. Moreover, after meticulous evaluation, the algorithm brought about captures the property of fine convergence rate in a contraction mapping way. Under some mild conditions, the proposed generalized information criterion (GIC$^*$) for selecting the sparsity level is consistent to find the truth. Combining HP with GIC$^*$ gives the adaptive procedure HP-GIC$^*$; HP-BIC denotes the same estimation method with sparsity selected by BIC. Finally, simulation studies show that GIC$^*$ improves support recovery relative to BIC in the reported comparisons, while HP achieves lower computational cost while maintaining estimation accuracy comparable to the sparse benchmark methods. A microfinance application illustrates the use of HP-GIC$^*$ for studying the association between network prominence and participation, with improved fit in the reported village-level regressions.

ml.title: Neural Networks and (Virtual) Extended Formulations
ml.abstract: Abstract. Neural networks with piecewise linear activation functions, such as rectified linear units (ReLU) or maxout, are among the most fundamental models in modern machine learning. We make a step towards proving lower bounds on the size of such neural networks by linking their representative capabilities to the notion of the extension complexity [Formula: see text] of a polytope [Formula: see text]. This is a well-studied quantity in combinatorial optimization and polyhedral geometry describing the number of inequalities needed to model [Formula: see text] as a linear program. We show that [Formula: see text] is a lower bound on the size of any monotone or input-convex neural network that solves the linear optimization problem over [Formula: see text]. This implies exponential lower bounds on such neural networks for a variety of problems, including the polynomially solvable maximum weight matching problem. In an attempt to prove similar bounds also for general neural networks, we introduce the notion of virtual extension complexity [Formula: see text], which generalizes [Formula: see text] and describes the number of inequalities needed to represent the linear optimization problem over [Formula: see text] as a difference of two linear programs. We prove that [Formula: see text] is a lower bound on the size of any neural network that optimizes over [Formula: see text]. While it remains an open question to derive useful lower bounds on [Formula: see text], we argue that this quantity deserves to be studied independently from neural networks by proving that one can efficiently optimize over a polytope [Formula: see text] given a virtual extended formulation with small encoding size.
ml.venue: SIAM Journal on Mathematics of Data Science

ml.title: External-Space-Participatory Three-Dimensional Generative Models: A Framework for Active Spatial Computation in 3D Generation
ml.abstract: Three-dimensional generative models typically represent objects, scenes, or spatial fields as the principal computational targets of generation. Spatial information outside a target object may be incorporated through conditioning, geometric constraints, scene representations, physical simulation, or environmental context. However, these approaches do not necessarily treat external space as an explicit computational substrate whose evolving state directly participates in the generation process. This paper proposes the conceptual framework of External-Space-Participatory Three-Dimensional Generative Models (ESPTGMs), in which the space surrounding a target object is modeled as an active computational domain rather than merely as background, an empty coordinate system, or a passive container. The proposed framework introduces a target representation, an external spatial field, a coupling mechanism, a spatial update operator, and a generation controller. Information can propagate through the external domain, interact with intermediate object representations, and influence subsequent geometric or appearance updates. The framework is representation-agnostic and may be instantiated using three-dimensional diffusion models, neural fields, point clouds, voxel grids, or hybrid representations. A mathematical formulation is developed to distinguish ordinary spatial conditioning from active external-space participation. Candidate objectives, implementation strategies, computational considerations, and an experimental protocol are presented. Because spatially aware scene generation and physics-guided generation already exist, the contribution is framed as a testable synthesis and formalization of a particular computational architecture rather than a claim that all constituent mechanisms are new. The central research question is whether explicitly stateful external-space computation can improve generation quality, geometric consistency, controllability, or computational efficiency relative to carefully matched baselines.

ml.title: User-Adaptive Generation of Generative AI Systems: A Framework for Generating Personalized Generative Artificial Intelligence from Individual User Requirements
ml.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) systems are commonly developed as general-purpose products that serve many users through shared model architectures, predefined capabilities, configurable settings, and standardized interaction interfaces. Although existing systems support personalization through prompts, memory, fine-tuning, retrieval, and tool integration, the underlying system is often designed before the individual user's requirements are fully known. This paper proposes User-Adaptive Generation of Generative AI Systems (UGGAI), a conceptual framework in which generative artificial intelligence is used to construct, configure, evaluate, and adapt generative AI systems according to the specific requirements of individual users. The central idea is to transform user requirements into explicit system-design specifications and then generate an appropriate AI system rather than merely generate content through an existing system. The generated system may differ in model selection, capability composition, interaction mechanisms, memory configuration, inference strategy, available tools, computational requirements, and adaptation policies. Depending on the user's needs, the result may be a personalized configuration of an existing model, a composed multi-model system, a parameter-adapted model, or a newly trained model when sufficient resources and evidence justify that approach. The framework further considers continuous adaptation, whereby changes in user requirements can trigger controlled regeneration or modification of the AI system. A formal problem formulation, reference architecture, user-requirement representation, generation procedure, evaluation methodology, and research hypotheses are presented. The framework is distinguished from conventional personalization, prompt optimization, recommender systems, automated machine learning, and user-specific model adaptation by its proposed focus on generating the AI system itself as an explicit design artifact. This distinction does not imply that the underlying techniques are individually new. Rather, the paper proposes a unified framework for investigating whether user-conditioned system generation can improve task satisfaction, usability, resource efficiency, and adaptability compared with fixed or manually configured alternatives. The framework remains a research proposal requiring implementation and empirical validation.
ml.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

ml.title: On the Convergence and Size Transferability of Continuous-Depth Graph Neural Networks
ml.abstract: Abstract. Continuous-depth graph neural networks, also known as graph neural differential equations (GNDEs), combine the structural inductive bias of graph neural networks (GNNs) with the continuous-depth architecture of neural ODEs, offering a scalable and principled framework for modeling dynamics on graphs. In this paper, we present a rigorous convergence analysis of GNDEs with time-varying parameters in the infinite-node limit, providing theoretical insights into their size transferability. To this end, we introduce Graphon Neural Differential Equations (Graphon-NDEs) as the infinite-node limit of GNDEs and establish their well-posedness. Leveraging tools from graphon theory and dynamical systems, we prove the trajectorywise convergence of GNDE solutions to Graphon-NDE solutions. Moreover, we derive explicit convergence rates under two deterministic graph sampling regimes: (1) weighted graphs sampled from smooth graphons, and (2) unweighted graphs sampled from [Formula: see text]-valued (discontinuous) graphons. We further establish size transferability bounds, providing theoretical justification for the practical strategy of transferring GNDE models trained on moderate-sized graphs to larger, structurally similar graphs without retraining. Numerical experiments using synthetic and real data support our theoretical findings.
ml.venue: SIAM Journal on Mathematics of Data Science

ml.title: Generative models for inverse problems
ml.abstract: Inverse problems are ubiquitous in scientific and engineering applications, where the goal is to recover an unknown signal from indirect and often corrupted observations. These problems are typically ill posed, requiring the incorporation of prior information to ensure stable and meaningful solutions. In recent years, deep generative models have emerged as powerful tools for encoding complex data distributions, offering a promising alternative to classical regularization techniques. This thesis investigates the use of generative models for solving inverse problems, with a particular focus on medical imaging applications and theoretical advancements in generative sensing. The work is structured into two main parts. In the first part, we address the problem of motion artifact correction in brain Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). We evaluate two primary applications of diffusion models: deploying them for direct motion correction, and utilizing them for data augmentation to generate synthetic pairs for supervised training. Through extensive numerical experiments on real MRI datasets, we quantitatively and qualitatively outline the strengths and weaknesses of these methods, while highlighting important considerations regarding model reliability and clinical applicability. The second part focuses on a theoretical extension of generative approaches to inverse problems. We introduce an infinite dimensional formulation of generative compressed sensing, where signals are assumed to lie in the range of a generative operator rather than being sparse in some predefined basis. Within this framework, we establish recovery guarantees and analyze the role of the sampling strategy, showing how adaptive measurements informed by the generative model can significantly improve reconstruction performance. Finally we perform numerical experiments, including applications to function space, to support the theoretical findings. Overall, this thesis demonstrates that generative models provide a flexible and effective framework for tackling inverse problems, bridging the gap between practical applications and theoretical understanding, and opening new directions for data driven reconstruction methods.

ml.title: Generative Auto-Bidding with Unified Modeling and Exploration
ml.abstract: Automated bidding is central to modern digital advertising. Early rule-based methods lacked adaptability, while subsequent Reinforcement Learning approaches modeled bidding as a Markov Decision Process but struggled with long-term dependencies. Recent generative models show promise, yet they lack explicit mechanisms to balance exploration and safety, relying solely on action perturbations or trajectory guidance without a safety fallback. This results in inefficient exploration and elevated financial risk for advertising platforms. To address this gap, we propose GUIDE (Generative Auto-Bidding with Unified Modeling and Exploration), a framework that synergistically integrates directed exploration with a safe fallback mechanism. GUIDE employs a Decision Transformer (DT) to jointly model historical bidding actions and environmental state transitions. A Q-value module guides the DT's exploration via regularization constraints, while an Inverse Dynamics Module (IDM) leverages DT-predicted future states to infer robust, behaviorally consistent actions as a safe policy fallback. The Q-value module then adaptively selects the final action between these two options, balancing exploration and safety. Together, these components form an integrated "explore-safeguard-select" pipeline that unifies efficiency and safety. We conduct extensive experiments on public datasets, in simulated auction environments, and through large-scale online deployment on Taobao, a leading Chinese advertising platform. Results show GUIDE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across all scenarios. In real-world deployment, GUIDE achieves notable gains: +4.10% ad GMV, +1.40% ad clicks, +1.66% ad cost, and +3.52% ad ROI, demonstrating its effectiveness and strong industrial applicability.

ml.title: Generative Modeling by Value-Driven Transport
ml.abstract: We propose a new framework for generative modeling based on a discrete-time stochastic control formulation of measure transport. Adapting classic results from control theory, we formulate our problem as a linear program whose dual variables correspond to the \emph{optimal value function} of the control problem, which directly encodes the optimal control policy. Exploiting this LP formulation, we develop an efficient simulation-free primal-dual algorithm for computing approximately optimal value functions and the associated \emph{value-driven transport} (VDT) policies which approximate the true optimal policy. We show that well-trained VDT policies enjoy numerous favorable properties in comparison with other state-of-the-art methods based on flows, diffusions, or Schrödinger bridges: they lead to straight transport paths which can be simulated quickly and robustly, and can be enhanced in all the same ways as diffusion and flow-based models (e.g., conditional generation, classifier-free guidance, unpaired data-to-data translation are all easy to incorporate). We evaluate our methodology in a range of experiments, with results that indicate strong performance and good potential for scalability.

ml.title: GenTac: Generative Modeling and Forecasting of Soccer Tactics
ml.abstract: Modeling open-play soccer tactics is a formidable challenge due to the stochastic, multi-agent nature of the game. Existing computational approaches typically produce single, deterministic trajectory forecasts or focus on highly structured set-pieces, fundamentally failing to capture the inherent variance and branching possibilities of real-world match evolution. Here, we introduce GenTac, a diffusion-based generative framework that conceptualizes soccer tactics as a stochastic process over continuous multi-player trajectories and discrete semantic events. By learning the underlying distribution of player movements from historical tracking data, GenTac samples diverse, plausible, long-horizon future trajectories. The framework supports rich contextual conditioning, including opponent behavior, specific team or league playing styles, and strategic objectives, while grounding continuous spatial dynamics into a 15-class tactical event space. Extensive evaluations on our proposed benchmark, TacBench, demonstrate four key capabilities: (1) GenTac achieves high geometric accuracy while strictly preserving the collective structural consistency of the team; (2) it accurately simulates stylistic nuances, distinguishing between specific teams (e.g., Auckland FC) and leagues (e.g., A-League versus German leagues); (3) it enables controllable counterfactual simulations, demonstrably altering spatial control and expected threat metrics based on offensive or defensive guidance; and (4) it reliably anticipates future tactical outcomes directly from generated rollouts. Finally, we demonstrate that GenTac can be successfully trained to generalize to other dynamic team sports, including basketball, American football, and ice hockey.

ml.title: Distance Marching for Generative Modeling
ml.abstract: Modern generative models based on diffusion or flow matching transport noise toward the data manifold, without representing the data manifold explicitly. We propose Distance Marching that explores an alternative design by explicitly modeling a distance field of the data manifold. A distance field offers a geometric view of generation as a descent process toward the data manifold using only the current position. The negative gradient of the distance field provides the direction, and the distance value can optionally determine the step size. However, sparse training data in high-dimensional space make it difficult to identify the closest points on the data manifold needed to train the distance field. To address this challenge, we design new loss functions that emphasize denoising targets from closer data points. Our analysis shows that, without time input, emphasizing closer targets reduces denoising ambiguity and the bias toward the data mean. This distance-field perspective naturally motivates two principled deterministic samplers, showing fast convergence in inference. As a result, our model is the only one without time input that remains competitive with time-conditioned models across datasets and architectures. Moreover, our distance prediction is also helpful for early stopping during sampling and for out-of-distribution detection. We hope distance-field modeling can open a promising direction for exploring generative modeling from a geometric perspective.

ml.title: An Adaptively Inexact First-Order Method for Bilevel Optimization with Application to Hyperparameter Learning
ml.abstract: Abstract. Various tasks in data science are modeled utilizing the variational regularization approach, where manually selecting regularization parameters presents a challenge. The difficulty gets exacerbated when employing regularizers involving a large number of hyperparameters. To overcome this challenge, bilevel learning can be employed to learn such parameters from data. However, neither exact function values nor exact gradients with respect to the hyperparameters are attainable, necessitating methods that only rely on inexact evaluation of such quantities. State-of-the-art inexact gradient-based methods a priori select a sequence of the required accuracies and cannot identify an appropriate step size since the Lipschitz constant of the hypergradient is unknown. In this work, we propose an algorithm with backtracking line search that only relies on inexact function evaluations and hypergradients and show convergence to a stationary point. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm determines the required accuracy dynamically rather than manually selected before running it. Our numerical experiments demonstrate the efficiency and feasibility of our approach for hyperparameter estimation on a range of relevant problems in imaging and data science such as total variation and field of experts denoising and multinomial logistic regression. Particularly, the results show that the algorithm is robust to its own hyperparameters such as the initial accuracies and step size.
