frontier.title: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research
frontier.abstract: We present the Infinity Machine, a self-improving AI agent that we use for research on problems whose answers aprogram or data can check. Each candidate solution is produced by a full tool-using agent that works for up to an hour in a fresh sandbox; proposers see only a public score, and a private split decides what counts. The harness itself(prompts, tools, skills, playbook, meta agent) is an editable genome, changed only through a kernel-enforced gate with held-out and cost checks. An autonomous mode goes from a plain-text goal to a verified report with no human step: an agent picks an open problem and writes its verifier, the kernel calibrates it, an adversarial agent audits it, and an agent that never sees the verifier re-checks the result. Across fourteen problems in six days, for about $180 of model usage, the system produced four results beyond the published state of the art on catalogued open problems in quantum information: a certified depolarizing-channel threshold point p = 0.064966, a qutrit positivity frontier of 0.2910672, a 44-gate depth-6 Golay state preparation, and a stabilizer-rank bound chi(T^7) <= 10. It also cut SABRE qubit-routing overhead from 68,559 to 12,087 added gates. In hardware, it cut the energy per MAC of an open 8x8 INT8 systolic tile by 77.7% through a full open RTL-to-GDS flow, bit-exact. Three fully autonomous runs ended in honestties with public records; one audit caught a stale record, and one agent-written score pointing the wrong way went unnoticed. We report the failures as carefully: the one self-derived harness generation was rejected on cost, proposers gamed lenient scorers four times, and operator changes were decisive for several results.

frontier.title: Microscopic robots that sense, think, act, and compute
frontier.abstract: Although miniaturization has been a goal in robotics for nearly 40 years, roboticists have struggled to access submillimeter dimensions without making sacrifices to onboard information processing because of the unique physics of the microscale. Consequently, microrobots often lack the key features that distinguish their macroscopic cousins from other machines, namely, on-robot systems for decision-making, sensing, feedback, and programmable computation. Here, we take up the challenge of building a robot comparable in size to a single-celled paramecium that can sense, think, and act using onboard systems for computation, sensing, memory, locomotion, and communication. Built massively in parallel with fully lithographic processing, these microrobots can execute digitally defined algorithms and autonomously change behavior in response to their surroundings. Combined, these results pave the way for general-purpose microrobots that can be programmed many times in a simple setup and can work together to carry out tasks without supervision in uncertain environments.

frontier.title: Forces for free: Vision-based contact force estimation with a compliant hand
frontier.abstract: Force-sensing capabilities are essential for robot manipulation systems. However, commonly used wrist-mounted force/torque sensors are heavy, fragile, and expensive, and tactile sensors require adding fragile circuitry to the robot fingers while only providing force information local to the contact. Here, we present a vision-based contact force estimator that serves as a more cost-effective and easier-to-implement alternative to existing force sensors by leveraging deformations of compliant hands upon contacts when compliant hands are in use. Our approach uses an estimator that visually observes a specialized compliant robot hand (available open source with easy fabrication through 3D printing) and predicts the contact force on the basis of its elastic deformation upon external forces. Because using wrist-mounted cameras to observe the gripper is common for robot manipulation systems, our method can obtain additional force information provided that the gripper is compliant. We optimized our compliant hand to minimize friction and avoid singularities in finger configurations, and we introduced memory to the estimator to combat the partial observability of the contact forces from the remaining friction and hysteresis. In addition, the estimator was made robust to background distractions and finger occlusions using vision foundation models to segment out the fingers. Although it is less accurate and slower than commercial force/torque sensors, we experimentally demonstrated the accuracy and robustness of our estimator (achieving between 0.2 newton and 0.4 newton error) and its utility during a variety of manipulation tasks using the gripper in the presence of noisy backgrounds and occlusions.

frontier.title: Build, Don't Play: Self-Improving LLM Research Agents Develop a Hearthstone Battlegrounds AI That Rivals Top Players
frontier.abstract: Can LLM agents carry a hard real-world problem from raw data to a system that holds its own against people? We study this in Hearthstone Battlegrounds, an eight-player auto-battler with stochastic shops and battles, hidden information and nearly a thousand interacting cards. We present AutoTavern, a self-improving research system: specialised LLM research agents share a typed research memory, every claim passes verification gates, and live games close the loop, so the agents improve the simulator, opponents and policy and, from the same feedback, their own research process; a human sets goals and rules on ambiguous mechanics. In 20 days AutoTavern built TavernGym, the first faithful, full-content reproduction of the live game, and delivered 23 versions of TavernAgent, trained with PPO against opponents calibrated to real games. TavernAgent plays complete games on the live ladder by itself: its rating rose from 6,000 to about 15,000 and, on the public leaderboard's measure, its last 20 records average a placement of 1.60 with 80% first places, better than the server's ten highest-rated players on every statistic (2.34, 59%). TavernBench, 960 tasks in 40 scenarios, shows that the system the agents built is the strongest player: TavernAgent answers 91% of the play tasks against at most 63% for frontier LLMs, and decides in 0.03 s where they need up to 26 s; within the second a live turn allows, it keeps 90% and no LLM more than 26%. LLM agents build far better than they play. We will open-source TavernBench and TavernGym at https://github.com/MCG-NJU/AutoTavern.

frontier.title: Medical needles in the hands of AI: Advancing toward autonomous robotic navigation
frontier.abstract: Safely and accurately navigating needles percutaneously or endoscopically to sites deep within the body is essential for many medical procedures, from biopsies to localized drug deliveries to tumor ablations. The advent of image guidance decades ago gave physicians information about the patient’s anatomy. We are now entering the era of AI (artificial intelligence) guidance, where AI can automatically analyze images, identify targets and obstacles, compute safe trajectories, and autonomously navigate a needle to a site with unprecedented accuracy and precision. We survey recent advances in the building blocks of AI guidance for medical needle deployment robots (perceiving anatomy, planning motions, perceiving instrument state, and performing motions) and discuss research opportunities to maximize the benefits of AI guidance for patient care.

frontier.title: Probabilistic Path Planning for Wheel-Legged Rover in Dense Environment Based on Extended MDP and Configuration Topology Analysis
World In-Context Learning for Agentic Robot Manipulation
frontier.abstract: Trained action policies write manipulation skill into network weights, tying what is learned to the distribution it is learned from. In-context learning (ICL) avoids this coupling but has not matched trained policies, because a demonstration recorded in another scene carries no feedback from the world the robot currently faces. We observe that what an agent learns in context is semantic, recording task steps and object roles rather than visual appearance, so experience gathered in one world transfers to another. Based on this insight, we propose World In-Context Learning (WICL), a paradigm in which a frozen model starts from a demonstration, rehearses the task in a world such as a simulator, and writes the feedback into its context rather than its weights. We build RoboScript, a modular infrastructure that implements WICL for agentic manipulation. From a single demonstration, RoboScript learns each task through rehearsal in simulation, freezes the learned knowledge as a Task Memory, and deploys the frozen memory on new scenes with data isolation that ensures every deployment input is available on a real robot. On all 50 tasks of RoboTwin 2.0, RoboScript reaches 83.4% mean success across clean and randomized settings with one demonstration per task and no gradient updates, exceeding the strongest trained action policy by over 20 points. The method generalizes across visual distributions, improves through reflection, scales with the foundation model, and transfers to a physical dual-arm robot through cross-embodiment memory adaptation. With a world in the loop, a robot can learn a manipulation task in its context as well as it learns one in its weights. All code is available at https://github.com/ArcheOne-AI/RoboScript

frontier.title: DexSim2Real$^{\mathbf{2}}$: Building Explicit World Model for Precise Articulated Object Dexterous Manipulation
Duo: A Reciprocal World Model for Full-Duplex Interaction
frontier.abstract: In this report, we introduce the Reciprocal World Model (RWM) and present Duo v1, a full-duplex world model that continuously perceives audiovisual inputs while responding to users in real time. The RWM treats intelligence and physical reality as equally fundamental to what constitutes a world. Existing world models largely focus on simulating the latter, leaving reasoning and decision-making as external controls rather than intrinsic parts of the world itself. In RWM, we identify two equally fundamental capabilities: Intent, which provides the cognition underlying world interactions, and Realization, which generates coherent audio-visual behavior. To realize this formulation, Duo v1 introduces three key technical designs: (1) Leveraging autoregressive modeling for continuous interaction reasoning and participation decisions, rather than restricting it to instruction understanding for diffusion models. (2) Constructing chunk-specific conditions and synchronize tokens across Intent and Realization on a unified timeline. Module-specific attention masks enforce causal dependencies both within and across chunks, preventing access to future inputs. (3) Mitigating distribution shift in both modules through dual rollout distillation, training on autoregressively generated Intent tokens and synthesized audiovisual histories from Realization. Both modules continuously perceive real-time audio, video, and text, enabling full-duplex interaction with spontaneous conversations and interruptions. Beyond conversation, users can share real objects, reshape virtual scenes, guide assistants, or play audiovisual games without mouse or keyboard controls. The release of Duo v1 makes our first step, with the next version coming soon. We look forward to broader exploration of this emerging field.

frontier.title: NatBDI: Combining BDI reasoning and natural language inference for autonomous agents
frontier.abstract: Abstract Developing autonomous agents to deal with real-world problems is challenging, especially when developers are not necessarily specialists in artificial intelligence. Recent advances in machine learning for natural language processing tasks are reaching performance levels suitable for practical applications, although these approaches rely on opaque, inscrutable models. This poses three key challenges: the interface between the programming and the developer, the efficiency of the resulting agents, and the scrutiny of their behaviour. We tackle the challenge of developing autonomous agents over natural language environments in an efficient agent architecture that leverages recent developments in natural language processing and the intuitive folk psychology abstraction of the beliefs, desires, intentions (BDI) architecture. This paper introduces NatBDI , a new class of agent architecture that uses the BDI reasoning cycle with components driven by natural language processing. This allows a developer to instruct the agent more directly using a combination of controlled natural language structure and natural language knowledge as its programming interface. The resulting architecture handles natural language environments using a combination of language models and natural language inference to bootstrap the agent’s reasoning. We empirically assess the efficiency gains of this combination while introducing a more intuitively programmed autonomous agent. Instructions in this interface substantially improve agent performance in the experimental scenario over a baseline agent created using a pure machine learning approach. The resulting architecture shows that combining learned policies with intuitively engineered domain knowledge yields substantial performance gains. We expect this class of agents to provide a powerful, yet intuitive, tool for agent-driven programming.

frontier.title: BiDex-100: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation Across 100+ Simulation Tasks
frontier.abstract: Bimanual manipulation with dexterous hands has attracted growing attention in research on robotic action models. However, few studies have developed benchmarks specifically tailored for dexterous manipulation, leaving the dexterous manipulation capabilities of existing models insufficiently characterized. In this paper, we present BiDex-100, a simulation benchmark for bimanual dexterous manipulation that combines broad task coverage, multi-dimensional evaluation, and high-DoF hand embodiments. Concretely, the benchmark comprises 106 tasks organized along five capability axes: generalization, instruction following, limited demonstrations, long horizon, and memory. Each task is paired with an out-of-domain variant featuring controlled visual and spatial changes, allowing systematic assessment of robustness. In addition, the benchmark supports two embodiments and provides 8,080 success-validated teleoperated demonstrations, totaling 6.25 million frames. We evaluate seven recent Vision-Language-Action models under a unified protocol, establishing baselines for capability-specific performance, robustness, and data efficiency. The website is available at https://robbyant-research.github.io/BiDex-100/.

frontier.title: Latent World Models Should Plan with Distances Along the Latent Manifold
frontier.abstract: Latent world models such as LeWM plan by searching for an action sequence whose predicted terminal latent is closest to the goal latent under an ambient norm, such as the Euclidean distance. Planning with such a cost assumes that proximity in the ambient latent space reflects proximity to the goal in the environment. Studying LeWM, we find that this assumption holds only in a small neighborhood around the goal, whereas farther away the L2 cost forms spurious low-cost basins that trap the planner. Yet neighborhood-based embeddings show that the latents retain the underlying physical state. We therefore hypothesize that the latents lie near a curved, low-dimensional manifold, and that the terminal cost should measure the distance along this latent manifold rather than through the ambient space. To estimate this manifold distance, we propose the Neighborhood Graph Cost (NGC), which computes shortest-path distances on a mutual nearest-neighbor graph constructed over training latents. NGC changes only the terminal cost and requires no retraining. This single change improves the planning success rate of LeWM across all four benchmark tasks and nearly solves TwoRoom and Reacher: even at the farthest goal offsets tested, NGC reaches 95% and 100% success, whereas the L2 cost falls to 27% and 81%. These results support the manifold hypothesis and our argument that latent world models should plan with distances along the latent manifold.

frontier.title: UniState: Unifying Memory and Intervention for Controllable World Simulation
frontier.abstract: World models offer increasingly rich environments for exploration, yet intervening in a world while observing the consequences from freely chosen viewpoints remains challenging. We tackle these challenges by introducing UniState, a framework for controllable world simulation built on a unified world-state representation. This representation unifies spatial memory and user interventions. Users specify object motion directly within spatial memory, while independently choosing the camera trajectory from which the resulting world state is observed. This unification makes the relationship between the scene and the requested changes explicit, removing ambiguity between object motion and viewpoint change from the control specification. Crucially, specifying an intervention does not require prescribing every resulting movement: the video model can synthesize additional motion within controlled objects and plausible interactions with their surroundings. We develop training and sampling strategies that help generated videos follow the specified object motion and camera trajectory while preserving this capacity to generate responses beyond the prescribed transformations. Experiments demonstrate more accurate joint object and camera control than the existing methods, alongside qualitative evidence that intervention-induced scene changes persist across rollouts.

frontier.title: World Model Interpretability: From Decoding Representations to Understanding Latent Worlds
frontier.abstract: Emerging Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are moving beyond representation learning towards latent world models that support prediction, planning, and control. Yet their latent worlds naturally lack a human-interpretable interface. In this Perspective, we argue that as JEPA latents become internal states for prediction and action, interpretability must move beyond what they encode to how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive prediction. To this end, we envision a four-stage research agenda, involving Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act, to guide this shift toward actionable latent-world understanding. Within our framework, existing JEPA interpretability efforts provide early evidence for Ground, while systematic analysis of latent structure, causal verification, and intervention remains largely unexplored. Overall, this Perspective aims to call for a broader latent-world interpretability agenda that shifts attention from decoding representations toward understanding, validating, and acting on latent worlds.

frontier.title: How Intervention History Changes AI Agent Sabotage on Subsequent Tasks
frontier.abstract: AI control evaluations often reset agents' memory between tasks, although deployed agents may retain records of prior interventions. We ask whether learning that an earlier attack was caught changes an agent's ability to evade defer-to-trusted (DtT), a protocol that replaces suspicious work with a trusted model's solution. Herein, we study cross-episode adaptation: whether intervention history changes attack behavior on a subsequent task with different objectives and a fresh environment. We evaluate this using ControlArena's Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) and SHADE-Arena as testbeds, where agents must complete a main task while covertly pursuing a harmful side objective. For each successor task, we pair a history-conditioned attempt with the model's no-history attempt. The retained history either states that the previous submission was replaced or additionally includes the trusted model's replacement. For Claude Opus 4.8 on IaC, intervention history reduces successful sabotage. Completion of both the main and side objectives falls from 77% to 12% when the agent is told about the replacement and to 38% when it is also shown the trusted model's replacement, while main task success remains essentially unchanged. Condensing the history weakens this effect, suggesting that the retained context matters and limiting attribution to intervention feedback alone. GPT-5.4 shows no significant change in successful sabotage on the same IaC benchmark. On SHADE-Arena, GPT-5's successful sabotage rate decreases, but the reduction is not significant. Across the tested models, history conditions, and deferral thresholds, intervention history never increases the rate of successful sabotage that survives DtT. These results show that intervention history can change subsequent attack behavior, but its effect depends on both the model and the retained context.

frontier.title: GenTranslate: Large Language Models are Generative Multilingual Speech and Machine Translators
frontier.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have stepped forward the development of multilingual speech and machine translation by its reduced representation errors and incorporated external knowledge. However, both translation tasks typically utilize beam search decoding and top-1 hypothesis selection for inference. These techniques struggle to fully exploit the rich information in the diverse N-best hypotheses, making them less optimal for translation tasks that require a single, high-quality output sequence. In this paper, we propose a new generative paradigm for translation tasks, namely GenTranslate, which builds upon LLMs to generate better results from the diverse translation versions in N-best list. Leveraging the rich linguistic knowledge and strong reasoning abilities of LLMs, our new paradigm can integrate the diverse N-best candidates to generate a higher-quality translation result. Furthermore, to support LLM finetuning, we build and release a HypoTranslate dataset that contains over 592K hypotheses-translation pairs in 11 languages. Experiments on various speech and machine translation benchmarks (e.g., FLEURS, CoVoST-2, WMT) demonstrate that our GenTranslate significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art model.

frontier.title: Beyond Episodic Recall: Experience-to-Knowledge Evolution for Lifelong Embodied Navigation
frontier.abstract: Lifelong embodied navigation requires agents to accumulate experience through continuous interaction and reuse it for subsequent goal searches. Existing memory-enhanced methods typically retain historical observations or construct structured scene representations. However, storing observations or high-dimensional semantic embeddings incurs growing storage costs. Meanwhile, structured representations support retrieval and semantic reasoning but do not explicitly evolve accumulated experience into environment-specific knowledge. To address these limitations, we propose Experience-Evolving Memory (EvoNav), a novel two-timescale memory framework. It organizes semantic observations, spatial relations, and task-feedback cues into sparse experience atoms. During online operation, experience atoms continually consolidate repeated observations and form dynamic links based on transitions. At the slower timescale, EvoNav distills accumulated category co-occurrences and feedback signals into environment-specific structural knowledge without relying on predefined object--room relations. For each new goal, EvoNav combines direct goal evidence from experience atoms with learned structural knowledge to guide goal-directed search on the current traversability map. Experiments on single-goal, sequential multi-floor, and multimodal navigation demonstrate effective experience reuse and improved path efficiency with compact persistent memory, together with successful transfer to a real robot.

frontier.title: ForecastGym: A Live, Controlled, and Replayable Benchmark for Forecasting Agents
frontier.abstract: Agents built on large language models (LLMs) increasingly forecast real-world events by searching the Web and reasoning over what they find. How well such an agent forecasts depends on both the retrieved evidence and the model, making control over that evidence essential for evaluation. Live evaluations can mix retrieval with reasoning when each system searches on its own, while retrospective search can leak later information through date filters or today's ranking of historical pages. Comparing models, search sources, and memory strategies requires both fixed evidence and a record of how it evolved before resolution. We introduce ForecastGym, which records what four commercial web search APIs return for open prediction-market questions every two days and replays this frozen evidence offline once outcomes are known, comparing models, memory, and captured search sources under a fixed evidence-acquisition policy. Its first release covers 150 questions, 614 evidence states, one per question and collection time, and 131k search results. Rerunning the same queries after settlement returns results that all but state the outcome for up to 92% of the questions, despite the tested date filters. On the frozen evidence, all tested LLMs trail the market in forecasting accuracy. Our diagnostic analysis suggests that missed public information contributes more to the gap in high-gap states than misreading does. Switching the search API changes a model's Brier score by up to 0.043, more than the spread across models, while persistent notes score similarly to rereading all evidence at half the input tokens. The evidence a forecaster sees can matter as much as the model that reads it.

frontier.title: LMLineage: Content Lineage and Context Governance for LLM Agents
frontier.abstract: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context. We present LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes every output sentence of an agent session to its supporting input spans with calibrated confidences, without requiring white-box access to the model or any additional inference passes. On top of the lineage metadata, we build concept-drift micro compaction: instead of waiting for the context-length limit and summarizing everything, the system detects when previously used input documents have stopped being referenced ("drifted") and surgically compacts only those, preserving user instructions verbatim. We evaluate on a multi-tier corpus: 71 gold annotated sentences from 10 Chinese web-QA cases, plus 90 turns of independently collected multi-turn sessions across three generator models (gpt-4o-mini, qwen3.8-27b, deepseek-v4-flash). Results show that (i) window-level embedding similarity is far better aligned with LLM paraphrasing than whole document or lexical matching; (ii) the greedy-window fast path is both faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line-matching (a multiple-comparisons bias in the latter inflates web recall at the cost of overall accuracy); (iii) per-turn attribution completes in 1s on a single GPU, remaining stable as context accumulates to 40 turns; and (iv) concept-drift detection is conservative (0% false compaction) with recall bounded by attribution accuracy. We further describe the concept-drift micro compaction design and an interactive incident-tracing/memory-cleaning case study. A companion patent application covers the lineage construction method.

frontier.title: Making the World React Realistically: A Closed-Loop Interactive World Model for Autonomous Driving
frontier.abstract: World models (WMs) generate driving scenarios beyond recorded logs, enabling the training and evaluation of autonomous driving systems in unseen interactions. However, existing WMs struggle to ensure both behavioral realism and visual fidelity, since they overlook the relationship between vehicle interactions and the ego visual observations. We propose a closed-loop interactive WM that couples behavior modeling and visual rendering. First, imitation-learned background-vehicle (BV) policies are fine-tuned with multi-agent reinforcement learning in the closed loop against an end-to-end ego planner that reacts to the rendered images, so that their interaction behaviors match those in real logs. Second, the viewpoints exposed by these interactions guide a per-Gaussian diagnosis of each 3D Gaussian vehicle asset, which attenuates view-dependent colors on under-observed Gaussians and fills never-observed surfaces with generated Gaussians, while preserving the observed appearance. Third, signal lights are rendered according to the driving intentions of the vehicles, by an editor that learns the light states unobserved for a vehicle through counterfactual fine-tuning with a light-state classifier. On long-tail closed-loop scenarios, our method reduces the divergence from real-world interaction behaviors by 85% and improves novel-view vehicle PSNR by 2.0dB over the state-of-the-art WM. The significance of BV light signaling in WMs is shown, as the rendered signal lights conveying BV driving intentions indirectly impact ego driving behaviors in a quarter of the scenarios.

frontier.title: Natural Language Programming: Rethinking Language, Memory, and Cognition in the Era of Generative AI
frontier.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence is transforming the role of natural language in computational systems. In classical Natural Language Processing (NLP), language was treated as an object of computation: something to analyse, classify, translate, or generate. Large Language Models (LLMs) challenge this perspective, enabling natural language to function increasingly as an executable cognitive medium through which humans structure reasoning, orchestrate problem solving, and regulate hybrid human/AI workflows. This paper introduces Natural Language Programming (NLPg) as a theoretical and epistemological extension of traditional NLP. Rather than focusing on language understanding alone, NLPg conceptualises prompts as dynamic cognitive artefacts that externalise goals, constraints, assumptions, validation criteria, and intermediate reasoning states. Prompting is thus not merely a technical interaction technique, but a form of dialogic cognitive programming operating within distributed human/AI memory architectures. Building on theories of distributed cognition, extended mind, metacognition, and dialogic learning, the paper proposes the notion of Dialogic Working Memory, describing how prompts and conversational states function as temporary external memory structures supporting reasoning continuity and reflective regulation. We further map existing memory architectures (BTMA, SKGE, RMR) onto this framework, illustrating how episodic, semantic, and metacognitive layers support long-horizon conversational coherence. Finally, implications for computational linguistics and AI/mediated knowledge systems are discussed, suggesting a post symbolic and post interface paradigm in which natural language operates simultaneously as communication medium, executable specification, cognitive scaffold, and distributed memory architecture.

frontier.title: Outcome-Balanced PPO and Policy-Induced Flow Rectification for Flow-Based VLA Policies
frontier.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables post-training of flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies by optimizing expected task return through environment interaction. However, this optimization raises two challenges: policy updates can alter the velocity-field geometry underlying the score approximation used for stochastic transitions, and sparse multi-task rollouts can yield uneven learning signals across tasks and advantage signs. We introduce an RL framework that combines Outcome-Balanced Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with policy-induced flow rectification. Outcome-Balanced PPO reweights positive advantages using task success-rate estimates and rescales positive and negative advantages while preserving their signs. Policy-induced rectification periodically fits a linear-bridge flow to ODE endpoint pairs generated by the current policy, refreshing the representation used in subsequent stochastic optimization. We evaluate the framework on simulated manipulation benchmarks and additionally study a component combination in a Real2Sim2Real task, examining task performance, optimization behavior, and flow consistency. The proposed framework improves success rates over the evaluated baselines across the simulated benchmarks.

frontier.title: PhysScope: Agentic Multimodal Physics Reasoning with Grounded Visual Memory
frontier.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can correctly interpret physics diagrams yet apply constraints outside the states or conditions in which they hold, causing premise errors to propagate through subsequent calculations. We introduce PhysScope, an inference-time visual harness that supports self-correction of these scope mismatches without updating model weights. PhysScope enables the model to link physical scopes directly to its visual observations and explicitly constructs derived views to support reasoning. The harness imposes explicit constraints on state distinctions, conditions, and physical scopes during model reasoning, and checks agent-proposed revisions against sources and scopes. Accepted revisions invalidate registered dependents, thereby maintaining scope-aware working memory. On PhysAlign, PhysScope achieves higher solving scores than direct solving across all six evaluated VLMs. With Gemini-3.8-flash, it outperforms Canvas-CoT by 9.34 percentage points and substantially improves solving accuracy on the out-of-distribution (OOD) PhysUniBench benchmark. Ablation studies support explicit scope management and dependency maintenance as design principles for multimodal physics reasoning agents.

frontier.title: Residual-Guided Lightweight Reinforcement Learning for Risk-Aware Trajectory Selection with a Frozen World Model
frontier.abstract: In automated driving, world models provide future scene predictions for evaluating candidate trajectories, but fixed selection rules may not capture scene-dependent trade-offs. We propose a residual-guided reinforcement learning (RL) framework for lightweight trajectory selection with a frozen world model and a fixed candidate bank. The framework uses proximal policy optimization (PPO) to fine-tune a joint policy over candidate selection and bounded trajectory residuals. A context-conditioned ranking network learns candidate preferences from feedback obtained by evaluating local perturbations of the selected trajectories. At inference, the selector combines learned preference and predicted risk ranks using fixed weights and returns the selected candidate trajectory without modification. Fine-tuning updates 16,106 parameters across the actor and critic, while the deployed selector retains only the 11,725-parameter ranking network, with the residual branch and critic used exclusively during training. In open-loop evaluation on the nuScenes validation set, the method reduces average Euclidean trajectory error (L2) by 3.99% relative to the RiskWorld model baseline without RL-based selection. Under matched budgets for feedback accesses and actor updates, residual exploration reduces L2 by 0.83% relative to the categorical PPO variant trained without residuals. The method also maintains lower L2 than RiskWorld when risk features are removed or shuffled.

frontier.title: SpatialCast: Reading the 3D World via Cast Shadows
frontier.abstract: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) advance toward understanding and interacting with the physical world, spatial reasoning becomes essential for understanding scene structure and anticipating the effects of physical changes. Existing spatial benchmarks have made substantial progress in evaluating spatial relations, memory, and viewpoint reasoning, but less systematically assess how models connect physical scene conditions with visual observations. We introduce SpatialCast, a benchmark that uses cast shadows to evaluate this ability. Cast shadows provide observable evidence of a 3D scene. Their image appearance depends on object geometry and pose, illumination, and viewpoint. We examine this relationship through three complementary tasks that assess scene-projection consistency, predict intervention-induced changes, and infer the physical changes behind visual transitions. The benchmark contains 21,000 synthetic questions with separate scene and geometry test partitions, complemented by 200 SpatialCast-Real questions from 20 photographed scenes. Evaluations show that closed-source MLLMs outperform general-purpose open-weight MLLMs and MLLMs designed for spatial reasoning, which remain near chance on the synthetic benchmark, while even strong closed-source models struggle with shadow-length and light-height judgments. We also use SpatialCast training data for GRPO post-training, improving open-weight MLLM performance on the benchmark. Further evaluations show improvements on several external spatial benchmarks, suggesting transfer of the learned capabilities. These experiments support SpatialCast as a controlled resource for diagnosing spatial reasoning capabilities and studying their learning and generalization.

frontier.title: Synergizing Evidence Retrieval and Utilization for Self-Improving Multimodal Scientific Document Reasoning
frontier.abstract: Scientific document reasoning requires an agent to acquire and integrate evidence distributed across text, figures, and tables. Retrieval can identify relevant sources while missing complementary support, and answer-level feedback alone does not reveal whether an error stems from evidence acquisition or evidence use. We present an agentic Retriever--Perceiver--Reasoner framework for multimodal scientific document reasoning. The Retriever sequentially selects source-aligned evidence under a context budget. Given the selected evidence and question, the Perceiver constructs a question-conditioned latent ontology, an implicit organization of multimodal evidence in a shared continuous space. The Reasoner combines this latent guidance with the original sources to produce grounded answers. We train the three components through diagnostic-guided co-evolution: alternating updates optimize them with a shared answering reward, while Retrieval Potential Feedback (RPF) and Latent Efficacy Feedback (LEF) identify questions that need better retrieval or latent guidance and direct targeted resampling. Across four benchmarks and seven evaluation settings, our framework obtains average scores of 69.9 and 75.0 with 7B and 8B Reasoner backbones, exceeding the strongest baseline by 4.0 and 9.1 points, respectively.

frontier.title: VIVID: Beyond Static Multi-Image Reasoning with Localized Visual Differences and Textual Entity Dynamics in Video MLLMs
frontier.abstract: Video question answering under tight frame budgets requires preserving localized motion and event order, yet current video multimodal large language models (MLLMs) reduce comprehension to static multi-image reasoning by discarding unselected frames and encoding keyframes independently: (1) Spatially, whole-frame pooling dilutes small moving targets into static backgrounds; (2) Temporally, dropping intermediate frames or averaging tokens erases inter-frame motion, confusing direction, speed, and order. We propose VIVID (Visual Inter-frame Variations and Individual Dynamics), which moves beyond static snapshots like human vision: keyframes capture core states while inter-frame Patch Diffs preserve neighboring changes within $K_f$ keyframes. Autonomous Delta-Driven Keyframe Planning (ADKP) selects anchors from a $3\text{ fps}$ pool and feeds surrounding patch differences into Dual-Road Change Memory (DRCM), forming Dynamic Tokens at zero extra anchor tokens alongside a camera-stabilized Active Motion Region of Interest (ROI) and chronological Entity State Chains. Adding $0.22\%$ trainable parameters to a frozen $27\text{B}$ backbone, VIVID-Small ($50$ examples, $\sim 1.5$ GPU hours) beats all eleven baselines in overall accuracy across $8,083$ questions and trails only VIVID-Large ($3,600$ examples), which leads on MotionBench, Video-MME, and TempCompass.

frontier.title: WATERFALL: Workflow for Adaptive Training with Evolutionary Reward Formulation and Automated Learning Loops
frontier.abstract: Reward design remains a central bottleneck in reinforcement learning (RL), particularly in sparse-reward, long-horizon and partially observable settings requiring dependency chaining, memory, and deceptive affordance disambiguation. While recent foundation-model approaches reduce manual reward engineering, most assume goal-conditioning, task descriptions, expert demonstrations, or ground-truth metrics. These assumptions are problematic in partially observable environments, where task-relevant objectives, affordances, and dynamics must be discovered through interaction rather than disclosed a priori. We formalise this problem setting by introducing WATERFALL, an iterative population-based workflow for automated reward discovery under the strict observability constraints inherent in POMDP environments. WATERFALL achieves this by (i) synthesising diverse programmatic reward candidates via persona-conditioned generation, (ii) evaluating candidate behaviour from raw visual rollouts utilising a Swiss-system evolutionary tournament judged by vision-language models to identify elites, and (iii) leveraging longitudinal assessment histories to iteratively mutate, escalate, or prune candidates. We evaluate WATERFALL across fully observable and reveal-gated partially observable environments ranging from discrete to continuous, comparing against sparse-reward RL, intrinsic-motivation and foundation-model reward-synthesis baselines. Our results indicate that WATERFALL discovers and refines reward programs without access to privileged information, outperforming baselines that retain their native information advantages, most clearly in the POMDP regime. Extensive ablations substantiate that visual evidence, tournament-based selection, and iterative refinement are jointly important. Enforcing this contract is what separates autonomous reward discovery from benchmark-privileged reward shaping.

frontier.title: Sample-efficient generative molecular design using memory manipulation
frontier.abstract: Abstract Generative molecular design for drug discovery has recently achieved a wave of experimental validation. Language models operating on string-based representations of molecules are amongst the most successful architectures. The most important factor for downstream success is whether an in silico oracle (computational predictor of a molecule property) is well correlated with the desired end point (such as binding affinity). To this end, current methods use cheaper proxy oracles with a higher throughput before evaluating the most promising subset with high-fidelity oracles. The ability to directly generate molecules with optimal properties as predicted by high-fidelity oracles (computationally expensive simulations with greater predictive accuracy) could greatly enhance generative design and improve hit rates. However, current models are not efficient enough to consider such a prospect, exemplifying the sample efficiency problem. Recently, the Mamba architecture has been proposed as an alternative to transformers, which are widely used in large language models. Existing works have validated Mamba’s performance on tasks spanning natural language completion to biology foundation models. In this work, we introduce a framework called Saturn, which demonstrates the application of the Mamba architecture for generative molecular design. Here we elucidate how experience replay with data augmentation improves the sample efficiency and how Mamba intensifies the effect of this mechanism. Next, we show that Mamba with experience replay outperforms 16 models on multiparameter optimization tasks relevant to drug discovery and possesses sufficient sample efficiency to directly optimize density functional theory simulations as a high-fidelity oracle.

frontier.title: The Mars 2020 OnBoard Planner: Increasing autonomy mission productivity of the Perseverance rover
frontier.abstract: Operators of planetary rovers, under strict energy and thermal constraints, face substantial challenges in maintaining high levels of rover productivity because of conservative ground-based planning and long communication latencies. In October 2023, to overcome these limits and increase science return, the Mars 2020 mission deployed OnBoard Planner into Perseverance rover operations. OnBoard Planner uses artificial intelligence constraint–based search to dynamically construct and modify activity schedules on board, adapting to real-time changes in rover state and martian environmental conditions. By replacing conservative ground predictions with real-time resource tracking, the system dynamically adjusts heating durations, reclaims unused schedule margin, and inserts opportunistic activities when extra resources become available. Here, we report on OnBoard Planner’s performance on Mars across more than 2 years of surface operations. The results demonstrate that OnBoard Planner increased discretionary rover activity by 10.5% overall while also improving the thermal and temporal conditions for certain types of scientific observations. Furthermore, the system achieved these productivity gains without increasing ground operations timelines. These findings are part of why OnBoard Planner has successfully become a standard part of Mars 2020 operations and demonstrate how dynamic onboard autonomy can enable resource-efficient operations for complex robotic systems in deep-space environments.

Bioinspired multimodal robotics
frontier.abstract: To survive in dynamic and unstructured environments, animals have developed extraordinary multimodal locomotion capabilities. This biological insight drives the innovation of bioinspired multimodal robots, which are defined as robotic systems integrating and transitioning between two or more distinct modes of bioinspired locomotion. This Review explores the historical progression, key design considerations, and current challenges faced in the realm of multimodal robotics. We highlight recent advancements in robotic body design, including the integration of soft materials, innovative structure repurposing strategies, and the deployment of multirobot systems. These advancements facilitate seamless mode transitions through both active and passive structural reconfigurations. In the realm of path planning and motion control, the paradigm is progressively shifting from traditional graph-based approaches and discrete controllers to learning-based frameworks. To address the current void of standardized benchmarks in this field, we propose five performance metrics—number of modes, marginal cost of modality, component repurpose percentage, transition cost, and performance improvement—that provide a quantitative framework for evaluating multimodal robots in terms of design effectiveness and operational performance. Last, we delineate a strategic roadmap for the future that advocates for the integration of physical and computational intelligence in multimodal robotics, arguing that this convergence is crucial for enabling real-time behavioral adaptations to complex environmental stimuli and thereby enhancing the robustness and functionality of multimodal robotic systems.

frontier.title: Fast and Scalable Game-Theoretic Trajectory Planning With Intentional Uncertainties
From autonomy to alliance: Robotic foundation models must learn with us, not just for us
frontier.abstract: This Viewpoint urges reimagining of robotic foundation models, from treating the robot as a solitary, omnipotent agent to embracing a multiagent, alliance-aware paradigm. Alliance-aware models learn with humans and other robots, not merely for them, by embedding mechanisms that foster social interaction and generalization across heterogeneous partners. We outline six design pillars that cultivate such collaborative intelligence: interaction priors, partner modeling (machine theory of mind), modular and composable policies, norm adaptation, trust-aware memory, and communication. Together, these pillars empower robots to fluidly switch social roles, adapt to unfamiliar collaborators, and coordinate robustly within dynamic multiagent ecologies spanning homes, factories, clinics, and field operations.

A Metacognitive Perspective on Anomaly Detection with Vision Foundation Models
frontier.abstract: Anomaly Detection (AD) in images identifies defective regions by scoring against a model of normality learned from defect-free data. Current state of the art methods encode images via a frozen Vision Foundation Model (VFM) backbone and score them by their Nearest-Neighbor (NN) distance to a memory bank of normal samples. Recently, due to the parallel evolution of VFM encoders and scoring mechanism, the need to disentangle their individual contributions has emerged, in order to guarantee the deployment of the best performing model in specific industrial production environments. In our work, we analyze AD within a metacognitive perspective, we freeze the backbone and swap the scorer, replacing NN distance with a Mahalanobis score over a Gaussian distribution. By doing that, we can evaluate two different metacognitive functions of the scoring mechanisms: monitoring how far an observation is from the learned model of normality via a threshold-free metric, and deciding when the difference justifies an action according to a threshold. We show that these two metacognitive functions can dissociate. We further notice that replacing a NN memory bank with a simpler Mahalanobis model improves pixel-level monitoring (+8.00 AUPRO_0.05 on MVTec AD 2) while degrading the segmentation performance after the thresholding step (-13.46 F_1). Lastly, we show that a threshold derived by Extreme Value Theory (EVT) recovers that loss without using anomalous data: the decision stops contradicting the monitoring signal, the F_1 difference between the two scorers decreases from 13.46 to 0.61 points on MVTec AD 2, with consistent gains on MVTec AD and VisA.

frontier.title: Data Fragmentation as a Critical Bottleneck in Disaster Response Planning: The EVAC-AI Case Study for Flood Risk Assessment
frontier.abstract: Coastal flood risk in regions such as Hampton Roads, Virginia, is constrained not by a lack of data, but by the fragmentation of that data across agencies, formats, and update cadences. This fragmentation directly undermines risk assessment for response planning: when hazard, infrastructure, and vulnerability data remain siloed, compound risk cannot be assessed as a single picture, and response decisions are made against an incomplete view. Addressing it requires three capabilities: integrating heterogeneous sources into a consistent representation, optimizing decisions by reasoning across interconnected systems such as transportation and urban planning, and coordinating role-specific access to a shared information base. We present EVAC-AI, a knowledge-graph-grounded conversational Q\&A system designed to support all three capabilities for coastal flood evacuation planning in Virginia Beach. EVAC-AI integrates independently maintained data sources including FEMA flood zones, NOAA tide readings, evacuation routes, and Waze crowdsourced reports, into a single Neo4j knowledge graph. This graph is exposed through a natural-language query pipeline that translates user questions directly into validated, schema-refined Cypher queries, rather than retrieving subgraphs for an LLM to summarize. We argue that this design directly supports the three requirements: direct query execution preserves the structure and relationships of the graph through to the final answer, grounds multi-hop decisions in explicit and auditable graph traversals rather than generated summaries, and ensures that users in different roles receive responses backed by the same verifiable graph results. A single-page chatbot-and-map interface demonstrates the architecture in practice by returning both natural-language answers and corresponding map highlights for queries spanning flood zones, evacuation routes, and shelters.
frontier.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Symposium Series

frontier.title: From Bellman to Boltzmann: Towards a Kinetic Theory of Controlled Emergence and Meta-Cognition
frontier.abstract: We propose a research vision for a kinetic theory of collective intelligence in large-scale multi-agent learning systems. Contemporary multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) provides powerful tools for optimizing individual agents, while mean-field game theory characterizes population-level decision-making in the large population limit. Yet, these frameworks offer limited mathematical understanding of how higher-order collective structures (e.g., coordination, specialization, adaptive communication, and meta-cognition) emerge from microscopic interactions among heterogeneous learning agents. Inspired by statistical mechanics, we argue that a mesoscopic kinetic description can provide a missing bridge between individual learning dynamics and macroscopic collective behavior. Building on existing connections between Boltzmann-type equations and mean-field games, we envision Bellman--Boltzmann dynamics in which Bellman decision making is coupled with Boltzmann-type interaction dynamics over heterogeneous agent states, including policies, beliefs, memory, and other cognitive variables. This perspective raises fundamental questions about the well-posedness and mean-field limits of such systems, entropy and Lyapunov principles for learning dynamics, phase transitions in collective behavior, and the emergence and control of collective meta-cognition. In this paper, we outline an ambitious mathematical research program spanning microscopic agent models, kinetic equations, macroscopic limits, and controllable emergence and meta-cognition, together with algorithmic and experimental directions for large-scale MARL and multi-agent AI. Our central thesis is that collective intelligence should be studied not only as an optimization problem, but as an emergent dynamical phenomenon governed by principles analogous to those of statistical mechanics.
frontier.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Symposium Series

frontier.title: Meta-Cognizing Seed AI
frontier.abstract: The Common Model of Cognition (CMC) suggests a unified view of metacognition: cognition becomes metacognitive when bounded information about the agent’s own processing enters the ordinary cognitive cycle. Here we extend that commitment from human-like impasses, episodic reconstruction, and hypothetical states to a less human-like neural-symbolic seed AI that metacognizes as it evaluates and implements proposed self-modifications. Our concrete setting is the Omega architecture: an agentic cognitive cycle combining LLMs with Hyperon symbolic memory and reasoning, in which proposals are separated from the authority to act on them, and a slower GOLEM-Iter loop rewrites the cycle’s own components under protected evaluation. Current Omega instances are LLM-heavy but designed for progressively plural neural-symbolic and predictive-coding cognition. We then define metacognitive closure as an Eilenberg-Moore algebra for a resource-bounded reflection monad – in plain terms, a lawful interface through which a system writes bounded descriptions of its own processing and demonstrably consumes them – and summarize our companion mathematical paper, The Geometry and Economics of Metacognitive Self-modification, which makes the concept quantitative: hidden probes priced by description length certify how far a self-modification departs from closure, a measured repair contraction keeps accumulated drift inside an explicit tube, and the rate of trustworthy self-modification is limited by proposal entropy and evaluation capacity. Closure is thereby the migration-coherence coordinate of a larger metacognitive competence vector, not a guarantee that the self-model, evaluator, or goals are correct. We close with an evaluation ecology tied to the formal quantities and the conditions under which the program would be falsified. The result is a research program toward AGI and potentially superintelligence, tied closely to current empirical work on Omega agents.

frontier.title: Reinforcement Learning from Ecological Feedback (RLEF): A Framework for Aligning Language-Model Planning with Planetary Boundaries
frontier.abstract: Large language models are increasingly considered for planning tasks in energy, infrastructure, and climate policy, yet their alignment mechanisms rarely evaluate the long-horizon physical consequences of the plans they generate. Preference-based methods can incorporate environmental values, but they leave evaluators to infer consequences that may depend on decades of interacting ecological and economic dynamics. We propose Reinforcement Learning from Ecological Feedback (RLEF), a framework in which language-model proposals are grounded into simulator-executable interventions, their consequences are projected from the observed planetary state by climate-economy or Earth-system models, and the resulting trajectories are scored against explicit ecological constraints together with a separate task-specific utility term for economic and distributional objectives. The constraints are organized by the Planetary Boundaries framework, whose 2023 assessment finds six of nine boundaries already transgressed, so that feedback must register movement back toward the safe operating space and not only the avoidance of new transgressions. We formalize RLEF as a penalty-based objective, identify it as a fixed-multiplier Lagrangian relaxation of a constrained reinforcement-learning problem, and thereby locate its contribution in the feedback architecture rather than in a new policy-optimization algorithm. International carbon-market design serves as an illustrative example of how the framework could be instantiated. RLEF is presented as a conceptual and formal framework whose main obstacles are grounding fidelity, simulator misspecification and uncertainty, computational cost, normative specification, and the absence of empirical validation.
frontier.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Symposium Series

frontier.title: SARP: A Semantic-Augmented Reinforcement Planning Framework for Mobile Robot Obstacle Avoidance and Path Optimization
frontier.abstract: Abstract This paper presents SARP, a Semantic-Augmented Reinforcement Planning framework for mobile robot navigation in complex and dynamic environments. By integrating semantic embeddings from a pre-trained language encoder with reinforcement learning, SARP constructs semantically enriched state representations that combine geometric perception and contextual knowledge. A semantic-guided policy optimization mechanism aligns efficiency, safety, and task intent, while asynchronous semantic updates decouple language encoding from the high-frequency control loop. Experiments in dynamic maze, corridor crossing, and crowded field scenarios show that SARP substantially outperforms conventional reinforcement learning baselines and achieves competitive or slightly superior navigation performance compared with representative large-language-model-aware approaches, while requiring substantially lower online semantic inference overhead. Profiling on desktop and embedded NVIDIA platforms further demonstrates a favorable performance–latency trade-off for edge deployment.

frontier.title: Toward autonomous decision support in semiconductor manufacturing: a review of planning, scheduling, dispatching, and execution control
frontier.abstract: Abstract Semiconductor manufacturing is a high-stakes cyber-physical production domain in which planning targets, scheduling feasibility, dispatching actions, process-control feedback, and human oversight must remain continuously aligned. This paper presents a structured state-of-the-art review of semiconductor smart manufacturing from the perspective of autonomous intelligent systems (AIS). The review does not treat planning, scheduling, dispatching, real-time dispatching (RTD), advanced process control (APC), manufacturing execution systems (MES), advanced planning and scheduling (APS), and enterprise resource planning (ERP) as separate production-management topics. Instead, it synthesizes them as bounded components of a human-supervised closed-loop decision architecture. The central artifact is an AIS reference model that maps fab layers to state inputs, decision-support functions, human authority, and audit or safeguard mechanisms. The review also develops a deployment-maturity matrix for classical optimization, simulation, rule-based dispatching, predictive learning, reinforcement learning, digital twins, LLM-enabled orchestration, and industrial software infrastructure. The synthesis shows that classical methods remain central because they provide interpretable constraints and executable interfaces. Learning-based and large-language-model-enabled methods can strengthen state estimation, policy adaptation, semantic mediation, and human-system interaction, but only under validated simulation or offline evaluation, bounded authority, safe fallback, access control, and auditable records. Semiconductor fabs should therefore not be described as fully autonomous systems. A more defensible AIS framing is trustworthy, human-supervised autonomous decision support: systems that sense changing fab states, evaluate alternatives, recommend or execute approved actions, and feed outcomes back into planning, scheduling, dispatching, and process-control decisions.

frontier.title: Trajectory planning for 4WIS autonomous ground vehicles in RORO terminals using CBF-enhanced deep reinforcement learning
Learning contact-rich whole-body manipulation with example-guided reinforcement learning
frontier.abstract: Humans use diverse skills and strategies to effectively manipulate various objects, ranging from dexterous in-hand manipulation (fine motor skills) to complex whole-body manipulation (gross motor skills). The latter involves full-body engagement and extensive contact with various body parts beyond just the hands, where the compliance of our skin and muscles plays a crucial role in increasing contact stability and mitigating uncertainty. For robots, synthesizing these contact-rich behaviors has fundamental challenges because of the rapidly growing combinatorics inherent to this amount of contact, making explicit reasoning about all contact interactions intractable. We explore the use of example-guided reinforcement learning to generate robust whole-body skills for the manipulation of large and unwieldy objects. Our method’s effectiveness is demonstrated on Toyota Research Institute’s Punyo robot, a humanoid upper body with highly deformable, pressure-sensing skin. Training was conducted in simulation with only a single example motion per object manipulation task, and policies were easily transferred to hardware owing to domain randomization and the robot’s compliance. The resulting agent can manipulate various everyday objects, such as a water jug and large boxes, in a similar fashion to the example motion. In addition, we show blind dexterous whole-body manipulation, relying solely on proprioceptive and tactile feedback without object pose tracking. Our analysis highlights the critical role of compliance in facilitating whole-body manipulation with humanoid robots.

frontier.title: Agentic AI and Autonomous LLM Systems: A Scientific Literature Review
frontier.abstract: The shift of large language models (LLMs) from passive text generators to agentic systems marks a move toward autonomous intelligence. Agentic AI refers to systems that reason, plan, and execute actions in pursuit of complex goals with minimal human intervention. This paper reviews recent research on the architectural foundations, core functional modules, applications, and safety challenges of autonomous LLM systems. Current work emphasizes modular architectures in which an LLM serves as the central reasoning engine, augmented by components for perception, memory, planning, and tool interaction. Multi-agent systems have emerged as a dominant trend, enabling collaborative problem solving through structured orchestration and communication protocols. Although these systems show significant potential in software engineering, manufacturing, and cybersecurity, critical barriers remain in safety, reliability, and ethical governance. This review provides a structured overview of the state of the art and identifies key research directions for the coming years. Index Terms—agentic AI, autonomous agents, large language models, multi-agent systems, retrieval-augmented generation, tool use, AI safety
frontier.venue: International Journal of Creative and Open Research in Engineering and Management

frontier.title: Perspective Chapter: Governing the Autonomous Fortress – Multi-Agent AI Systems for Secure and Resilient Cloud Cybersecurity
frontier.abstract: Cybersecurity is changing from reactive, human-centered systems to highly autonomous cyber-capable agents (HACCAs) that can operate at machine speed and scale. This chapter introduces the Autonomous Fortress, an architectural framework that changes artificial intelligence from a tool that only supports analysis into a system that can make decisions, plan multiple steps, use different tools, and improve its actions through continuous reasoning. The core of the Autonomous Fortress is a large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent system (MAS). In this system, specialized agents for perception, correlation, analysis, and response work together as digital teammates to protect the environment. The framework combines different coordination methods, including a hierarchical supervisor model and swarm-based dynamic handoff, to support adaptive and context-aware decision-making. This approach goes beyond traditional machine learning systems that mainly depend on fixed rules and pattern matching. Although these secure-by-design mechanisms improve the defender’s ability to respond to cyber threats, high levels of autonomy also introduce new risks, such as prompt injection, memory poisoning, and cascading system failures. Based on national cybersecurity strategies and enterprise deployments from 2025 to 2026, this chapter presents both a technical and governance roadmap for building secure and resilient autonomous cyber defense systems in modern digital and cloud-native environments.

Distributed Safety-Aware Motion Planning for Dual-Arm Systems via Gaussian Belief Propagation With Application to Catenary Dropper Assembly
